## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303)Abstract

Pulmonary embolism (PE) occurs when thrombi from deep vein thrombosis dislodge and obstruct pulmonary arteries, raising pulmonary artery pressure and straining the right ventricle. This strain can lead to right ventricular dysfunction (RVD), characterized by reduced cardiac output, impaired contractility, and potential development of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Clinically, PE may present with symptoms such as dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and tachycardia. Diagnosis is typically confirmed through computed tomography pulmonary angiography, biomarkers like D-dimer and cardiac troponins, and clinical scoring systems. Acute management focuses on hemodynamic support, including intravenous fluids and vasopressors, and may involve anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin or direct oral anticoagulants. Severe cases may require systemic anticoagulation, catheter-directed techniques, and surgeries like pulmonary endarterectomy. Long-term management involves continued anticoagulation tailored to individual risk factors, with ongoing monitoring to prevent recurrence. Effective early diagnosis and management are crucial, as severe PE can significantly increase mortality and lead to serious complications. This review explores the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of PE and RVD.

**Keywords:**anticoagulants, hemodynamics, heart ventricles, management, mechanisms, right ventricular dysfunction, pulmonary embolism

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303)Introduction and background

Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a severe and frequently life-threatening condition resulting from the obstruction of a pulmonary artery or its branches, typically due to a thrombus that has migrated from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF1)]. This obstruction disrupts blood flow to the lungs, causing an acute elevation in pulmonary arterial pressure. The resultant increase in pressure imposes substantial strain on the right ventricle (RV), the cardiac chamber responsible for propelling blood into the pulmonary circulation. As the RV attempts to manage the heightened workload, it may become overwhelmed, leading to right ventricular dysfunction (RVD). This dysfunction compromises the heart's ability to pump blood effectively, potentially resulting in reduced cardiac output, hypotension, and further systemic circulatory impairment. Significant hemodynamic compromise can occur in up to 8% of patients with acute PE. This condition is linked to a substantial rise in mortality rates, ranging from 15% to 42%, primarily due to acute right ventricular failure [[2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF2)]. Clinically, PE can present with acute symptoms such as sudden onset of dyspnea, sharp chest pain, tachycardia, and in severe cases, syncope or collapse [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF3)]. Long-term complications, including chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), can arise when elevated pulmonary pressures persist, leading to sustained RV impairment and ongoing cardiovascular strain [[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF4)].

The clinical significance of PE and RVD is substantial due to their impact on patient outcomes and healthcare systems. PE is a common disorder with an estimated yearly incidence of 0.7 to 1 per 1000 inhabitants in the Western world [[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF5)]. It is a leading cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality globally, with prevalence influenced by variables such as age, underlying health conditions, and lifestyle factors. RVD plays a critical role in the severity of PE and is associated with increased mortality and adverse outcomes. Patients exhibiting RVD face a higher risk of severe complications, including shock and death, and often require more intensive therapeutic interventions. In-hospital mortality due to PE ranges from 22.0% to 31.8%, increasing up to 65% in cases of cardiac arrest [[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF6)], with most deaths occurring within the first hour [[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF7)]. This highlights the critical need for early recognition and treatment. Research indicates that the presence of RVD is correlated with poorer prognosis and can complicate the management of PE, underscoring the importance of early detection and timely treatment [[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF8)]. A comprehensive understanding of the prevalence and impact of RVD in PE patients is essential for developing effective treatment strategies and enhancing patient outcomes. This review aims to comprehensively evaluate the mechanisms and management strategies associated with PE and RVD by analyzing the evidence from the current available literature. The objectives include examining the pathophysiological processes through which PE induces RVD, assessing the clinical impact of RVD on patient outcomes, and reviewing current treatment approaches.

## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303)Review

Discussion

Pathophysiology and Mechanism

Pulmonary embolism: Most PEs arise from thrombi in the deep veins of the lower extremities, primarily in the calf veins, followed by the femoropopliteal veins, and less frequently in the iliac veins. Thrombosis often occurs in areas with reduced blood flow, such as near valve cusps and at bifurcations, and can be exacerbated by local hypercoagulability due to factors like hypoxia and hemoconcentration [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF9)]. A smaller fraction of emboli originates from upper extremity veins, typically associated with central venous catheters, intracardiac devices such as pacemakers and defibrillators, malignancy, or trauma related to activity. Additionally, DVT in the pelvic veins can lead to PEs, especially when accompanied by risk factors such as pelvic infections, surgeries, or pregnancy. Central DVTs in the lower extremities are more likely to result in PE for 15%-32%, while those in the upper extremities have a lower incidence of PE approximately 6% [[9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF9)].

PE occurs when clots formed in the deep venous system break loose and travel to block the pulmonary arteries. Smaller PEs may resolve on their own, but larger clots can cause a rapid and significant increase in pulmonary arterial pressure, potentially leading to circulatory collapse. Clot formation often begins at sites of tissue or vascular injury, where activated monocytes expose tissue factor, disrupting the body’s natural anticoagulant and fibrinolytic processes. DVT composed mainly of red blood cells, platelets, and fibrin typically forms in the venous sinuses or valve cusps of the lower extremities. The primary risk is that part or all of a DVT could travel to the lungs. Moreover, the congestion caused by DVT can lead to swelling and discomfort in the affected limb, along with impaired valve function. This dysfunction can obstruct blood flow, resulting in increased swelling, venous stasis, and further thrombus formation [[10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF10)]. Risk factors include immobility, recent surgery, malignancy, pregnancy, and hormone use [[11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF11)]. Virchow's triad endothelial injury, hypercoagulability, and venous stasis play a role in thrombus formation [[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF12)]. The obstruction increases pulmonary artery pressure, burdening the RV and potentially leading to RV dysfunction and reduced systemic perfusion [[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF13)]. Chronic obstruction can cause pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular dysfunction.

Right ventricular dysfunction: PE leads to increased pulmonary artery pressure and afterload on the RV, which struggles to generate adequate pressure [[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF14)]. Increased pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) decreases RV stroke volume, causing acute dilation and impaired contractility, potentially leading to RV failure. Prolonged pressure overload can result in maladaptive RV remodeling, including dilation and reduced systolic function. Disrupted RV-arterial coupling affects contractility and relaxation, contributing to symptoms like peripheral edema and ascites [[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF3)]. The RV’s thin wall and low-pressure handling make it vulnerable to sudden increases in pressure. Acute PE leads to RV pressure overload through increased PVR and neurohormonal responses, even with low clot burdens [[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF15)]. Increased PVR causes decreased stroke volume and compensatory tachycardia, while fibrosis and inflammation further impair RV function [[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF16)]. RV dilation and interventricular septum displacement reduce left ventricle (LV) filling and systemic perfusion, exacerbating right-sided heart failure and creating a feedback loop of the RV and LV dysfunction.

Classification, Clinical Presentation and Diagnosis

The severity of PE is generally classified following the 2019 guidelines from the American Heart Association (AHA) and the European Society of Cardiology (ESC). These frameworks, which are quite similar, categorize PE into three main levels [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF17)]. PE is classified into three categories based on severity and risk factors. Massive; high-risk PE, which accounts for about 5% of cases, is characterized by hypotension, defined as a systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg or a significant drop in blood pressure for at least 15 minutes, often requiring vasopressor support; this group has a mortality rate of approximately 65% [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF17)-[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF19)]. Intermediate-risk; submassive PE accounts for about 40% of cases and includes patients showing signs of right ventricular strain, dilation, or dysfunction, with varying degrees of severity affecting mortality rates of 5-25% [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF17)-[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF19)]. Low-risk PE, which encompasses 40-60% of cases, involves patients who do not meet the criteria for the other two categories, resulting in a much lower mortality rate of around 1%. This classification helps guide treatment and management strategies for patients with PE [[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF17)-[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF19)].

PE is often referred to as the great masquerade, as it can present with a wide range of symptoms [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF20)]. Patients with symptomatic PE are at a greater risk for experiencing recurrent PE and fatal recurrent PE compared to those with DVT alone. Approximately one-third of individuals with acute DVT have asymptomatic PE. The prevalence of asymptomatic PE is roughly twice as high in patients with proximal DVT involving the popliteal vein or more proximal veins compared to those with distal DVT confined to the calf veins. Additionally, patients with unprovoked DVT are more likely to have asymptomatic PE than those with provoked DVT [[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF21)]. Commonly reported symptoms include dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, cough, and hemoptysis, while tachypnea and tachycardia are frequently observed signs. Additionally, other manifestations such as syncope and alterations in mental status may occur [[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF20)].Dyspnea ranges from mild to severe, while pleuritic chest pain is sharp and worsens with respiration. Tachycardia reflects the heart’s response to elevated pulmonary artery pressure and reduced cardiac output. Other signs include hypoxemia, jugular venous distention, and peripheral edema [[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF22)]. Atypical symptoms like syncope, hemoptysis, and nonspecific fatigue can complicate diagnosis. Chronic or recurrent PE may present as CTEPH with progressive dyspnea and right heart failure signs.

CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the primary diagnostic tool, offering high sensitivity and specificity through detailed imaging of the pulmonary arteries [[23](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF23)]. Despite its accuracy, CTPA requires careful consideration of contrast use and radiation exposure. Echocardiography, including transesophageal echocardiography and transthoracic echocardiography, provides insights into right ventricular function and thrombi presence, though it is less definitive than CTPA. Biomarkers such as D-dimer, cardiac troponins, and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) aid in diagnosis. D-dimer is sensitive but lacks specificity for PE. Elevated cardiac troponins indicate significant RV strain and worse prognosis, while BNP reflects RV dysfunction and heart failure [[24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF24)].Recently, several prediction rules have been developed to categorize patients with suspected PE based on clinical or pretest probability. Among these, the Wells score and the revised Geneva score are the most validated and widely utilized, stratifying patients into low, moderate, and high probability groups. While both scoring systems have proven valuable for accurate diagnosis, there is limited research focusing on elderly patients. As per Guo et al., the Wells score demonstrates superior diagnostic accuracy compared to the revised Geneva score for those with suspected PE. Additionally, combining either score with a normal D-dimer level is an effective strategy for safely ruling out PE [[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF25)].

The management of patients with intermediate and high-risk PE is a complex and often debated issue. With various treatment options available, determining the most appropriate approach can be challenging. Additionally, care for PE patients frequently involves multiple medical specialties. To streamline the response to acute PE cases, many hospitals and academic institutions have established pulmonary embolism response teams (PERTs). These teams consist of a multidisciplinary group of experts in thromboembolic disease who can quickly address the needs of patients with acute PE. The objective of a PERT is to develop a rapid, individualized treatment plan without the need to consult several different specialists, drawing inspiration from the structure of rapid response teams [[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF26)].

Management

The acute management of PE involves a comprehensive approach to initial assessment and stabilization, with a particular focus on hemodynamic support. Upon presentation, immediate assessment of the patient’s hemodynamic status is critical. This includes evaluating vital signs such as blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation, as well as assessing for signs of shock, hypotension, or right ventricular strain [[27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF27)]. The goal is to promptly identify and address any life-threatening conditions, such as severe hypotension or impaired cardiac output, which may require urgent intervention.

Hemodynamic support often involves the administration of intravenous fluids to maintain adequate blood volume and improve systemic perfusion. In cases where fluid resuscitation alone is insufficient to stabilize blood pressure, vasopressor agents may be required to augment cardiovascular function [[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF28)]. Commonly used vasopressors include norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dobutamine, which help restore adequate blood pressure and ensure sufficient perfusion of vital organs. The choice and dosage of these agents are tailored to the patient’s specific clinical condition and response to therapy. Additionally, a progressive rise in pulmonary arterial pressure caused by PE leads to ongoing deterioration in pulmonary artery hemodynamics, right ventricular function, right ventricular-pulmonary arterial coupling, and overall cardiac output. Levosimendan has been shown to more effectively restore right ventricular-pulmonary arterial coupling compared to placebo, primarily due to its dual effects of pulmonary vasodilation and enhanced right ventricular contractility [[29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF29)]. Levosimendan is a calcium sensitizer that exhibits inotropic, pulmonary vasodilatory, and cardioprotective effects [[30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF30)].

Historically, the management of high-risk PE has primarily centered on the prompt initiation of anticoagulation therapy, utilizing either unfractionated heparin (UFH) or low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH). The main objective of this approach is to prevent the further propagation of blood clots and their migration to other areas of the body. While effective in certain cases, this strategy has led clinicians to explore alternative methods that more aggressively address the clot burden [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF31)]. One such method is thrombolysis, which employs fibrinolytic agents to rapidly dissolve obstructive clots and restore pulmonary blood flow. However, the use of thrombolysis in MPE remains controversial. While it offers the potential for rapid clot resolution, there are significant concerns regarding the risk of bleeding, especially in hemodynamically unstable patients. This has led to ongoing debates within the medical community [[31](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF31)]. To evaluate the appropriateness of thrombolytic therapy, it is crucial to weigh the benefits of swift clot dissolution against the potential bleeding risks. This assessment should take into account individual patient characteristics, comorbidities, and the overall risk-benefit balance of the treatment. Conversely, reliance solely on anticoagulation presents limitations, as these medications primarily prevent further clot formation but may not sufficiently reduce the size of existing clots, potentially leading to ongoing circulation issues and associated complications [[32](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF32),[33](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF33)].

Administered subcutaneously, LMWH typically requires daily or twice-daily injections, with dosage based on patient weight and renal function. This approach is favored for its predictable pharmacokinetics and reduced need for routine monitoring. UFH is another option, particularly for patients with severe PE or those requiring rapid reversal of anticoagulation [[34](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF34)]. Unfractionated heparin is given intravenously, starting with a bolus dose followed by continuous infusion, with dosing adjusted based on activated partial thromboplastin time or anti-factor Xa levels. While UFH requires frequent monitoring and dose adjustments, it allows for rapid titration and is suitable for high-risk patients or those undergoing invasive procedures. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), such as rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban, are used for long-term management following initial therapy with LMWH or UFH [[35](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF35)]. These agents, administered orally, offer the advantage of fixed dosing and minimal need for routine monitoring. The transition from injectable anticoagulants to DOACs typically occurs after the initial stabilization period. Warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, has traditionally been used for long-term anticoagulation but requires careful monitoring of the international normalized ratio (INR) and is often overlapped with LMWH or UFH until therapeutic levels are reached [[36](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF36)]. Despite its effectiveness, warfarin's use has declined in favor of DOACs due to their convenience and reduced monitoring requirements. Each anticoagulant has specific protocols and considerations, with treatment choices tailored to the patient’s condition and clinical circumstances.

Administration of thrombolytics typically involves intravenous infusion of agents such as tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), including alteplase, which is the most commonly used thrombolytic agent for PE [[37](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF37)]. The standard protocol involves a bolus dose followed by a continuous infusion over a specific duration, generally 1 to 2 hours, depending on the agent used and patient characteristics. Close monitoring during and after administration is crucial to detect potential complications, including bleeding and allergic reactions, and to assess the therapeutic response. Dosage adjustments and supportive measures, including blood pressure management and hemostatic monitoring, may be necessary to ensure patient safety and maximize treatment efficacy. However, the use of thrombolytic therapy is associated with several contraindications that must be carefully evaluated to minimize the risk of adverse effects [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF38)]. Absolute contraindications include active bleeding or a recent history of bleeding disorders, intracranial hemorrhage, or recent major surgery, as these conditions significantly increase the risk of severe hemorrhagic complications. Other relative contraindications include a history of stroke or transient ischemic attack, uncontrolled hypertension, or significant trauma, which may warrant cautious consideration and thorough risk assessment before initiating therapy. However, the use of thrombolytic therapy is associated with several contraindications that must be carefully evaluated to minimize the risk of adverse effects [[38](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF38)]. In the management of severe PE, surgical and catheter-based interventions may be necessary, particularly when thrombolytic therapy is contraindicated, ineffective, or not feasible [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF1)]. These interventions aim to rapidly remove or dissolve thrombi to restore pulmonary blood flow and mitigate hemodynamic compromise. Embolectomy, a catheter-based procedure, involves the direct removal of emboli from the pulmonary arteries. It is typically considered in cases of massive PE or when there is a contraindication to thrombolytic therapy, such as a high risk of bleeding or when thrombolytics have failed to alleviate symptoms. The procedure can be performed via open surgery or minimally invasive techniques, such as catheter-based embolectomy. During open surgical embolectomy, a cardiopulmonary bypass is used to temporarily take over the function of the heart and lungs while the emboli are removed [[40](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF40)]. This approach is generally reserved for patients with severe hemodynamic instability or those who do not respond to other treatments. Minimally invasive techniques, such as the percutaneous approach, involve the use of specialized catheters and tools to remove thrombi through a small incision, often with a quicker recovery time and fewer complications compared to open surgery. Catheter-directed thrombolysis is a less invasive alternative to systemic thrombolysis and is used primarily for patients with intermediate-risk PE or those who are not candidates for systemic thrombolytics [[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF1)]. This technique involves the insertion of a catheter through a large vein, usually in the groin, which is then advanced to the pulmonary arteries. Thrombolytic agents, such as tPA, are delivered directly to the site of the clot via the catheter, allowing for targeted dissolution of the thrombus. The procedure may be performed using various methods, including mechanical thrombolysis devices that enhance the effectiveness of drug delivery or directly remove thrombi through mechanical means. The primary advantage of catheter-directed thrombolysis is its ability to reduce systemic bleeding risks compared to systemic thrombolysis while providing localized thrombus resolution [[41](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF41)].

Both embolectomy and catheter-directed thrombolysis require careful patient selection and consideration of risks versus benefits. These interventions are typically reserved for severe cases of PE where immediate restoration of pulmonary circulation is critical. Observational studies indicate that catheter-directed therapy may lower the risk of significant in-hospital bleeding compared to systemic thrombolysis, potentially leading to decreased in-hospital mortality and shorter stays in intensive care and overall hospital length. If ongoing prospective randomized trials confirm these positive outcomes, this could translate into cost savings that should be factored into future health economic evaluations. However, the direct costs associated with catheter-directed thrombolysis for advanced PE will need to be evaluated based on each country’s hospital reimbursement system. These costs should be considered alongside potential benefits, such as a reduction in early complications, earlier hospital discharge, improved return to work and productivity, and prevention of long-term issues [[42](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF42)].

Supportive Measures for RV Dysfunction

Supportive measures for RVD in the context of PE are essential for stabilizing patients and improving hemodynamic and respiratory function. These interventions aim to alleviate the strain on the RV and ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation. Oxygen therapy is a fundamental supportive measure for patients with RV dysfunction, particularly those with compromised oxygenation due to impaired pulmonary circulation [[43](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF43)]. Mechanical ventilation provides positive pressure ventilation to support or replace spontaneous breathing, thereby enhancing gas exchange and reducing the workload on the RV. The choice between invasive ventilation (endotracheal intubation) and non-invasive ventilation (such as bilevel positive airway pressure or continuous positive airway pressure) depends on the patient’s clinical condition and the degree of respiratory distress. Invasive mechanical ventilation may be necessary for patients with severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, altered mental status, or inability to protect their airway [[44](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF44)]. Proper ventilation settings are crucial to avoid ventilator-induced lung injury and to minimize hemodynamic instability. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation represents a more advanced supportive measure for patients with severe RV dysfunction, especially when conventional therapies are inadequate [[45](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF45)].

Long-term anticoagulation is a critical component in the chronic management of PE to prevent recurrent thromboembolic events and to manage the risk of further complications. The duration and monitoring of anticoagulant therapy are tailored to the individual patient’s clinical condition, the underlying risk factors, and the initial PE severity. The duration of anticoagulant therapy for patients with PE generally depends on whether the event was provoked or unprovoked. For patients with a provoked PE, such as one associated with a transient risk factor (e.g., recent surgery or prolonged immobilization), anticoagulation is typically continued for a period of 3 to 6 months. In cases of unprovoked PE, or when the initial event occurs in the absence of obvious risk factors, longer-term anticoagulation is often recommended [[46](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF46)]. This duration can extend from 6 to 12 months or even longer, depending on the patient's risk of recurrence and bleeding. For patients with recurrent PE, active cancer, or persistent risk factors, indefinite anticoagulation may be necessary. The decision to continue or discontinue therapy is based on a risk-benefit assessment, considering the potential for recurrent thromboembolism versus the risk of anticoagulant-related bleeding. Monitoring is essential to ensure the efficacy and safety of long-term anticoagulant therapy. For patients on warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist, regular monitoring of the international normalized ratio (INR) is required to maintain therapeutic levels and avoid complications such as bleeding or thrombosis [[47](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF47)]. The INR is typically checked every 1 to 4 weeks, depending on the stability of the patient's INR levels and any recent changes in medication or diet. Direct oral anticoagulants, including rivaroxaban, apixaban, and edoxaban, generally require less frequent monitoring, as these agents have predictable pharmacokinetics and dosing regimens. However, periodic assessment of renal function and adherence to therapy is recommended to ensure optimal dosing and effectiveness. For patients with renal impairment, dose adjustments and more frequent monitoring may be necessary.

Prognosis and Outcomes

The short-term prognosis following an acute pulmonary embolism and RVD is largely determined by the severity of the embolic event and the timeliness of therapeutic interventions. Patients with severe pulmonary artery obstruction and significant RV dysfunction are at heightened risk for acute morbidity and mortality. Rapid and effective management is crucial to improving immediate survival rates and mitigating adverse outcomes during the acute phase of the condition [[48](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF48)]. Long-term prognosis for individuals with a history of pulmonary embolism and RVD is influenced by several factors, including the resolution of the acute event, the presence of residual pulmonary hypertension, and the efficacy of ongoing management strategies. While many patients achieve substantial recovery, some may endure persistent symptoms, diminished exercise capacity, and a reduced quality of life [[49](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF49)]. A study by Farmakis et al. concluded that three months following PE, 37% of patients experienced dyspnea, while 22% exhibited abnormal six-minute walk distance (6MWD). After one year, 20% continued to show abnormal 6MWD. There was a correlation between dyspnea and abnormal 6MWD, yet over half of those with abnormal 6MWD did not report experiencing dyspnea. Abnormal 6MWD was a significant predictor of later impairment and a decline in long-term quality of life after PE [[50](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF50)].

Additionally, studies with varying methodologies have shown that residual perfusion defects can be identified in up to 50% of patients six months after a PE through ventilation-perfusion lung scans. Approximately half of these patients continue to experience persistent symptoms and cardiopulmonary functional limitations for up to one-year post-PE. While there has been a growing focus on the long-term hemodynamic and functional effects of acute PE, the impact on patients' psychological and emotional well-being, as well as their quality of life, remains under-researched. Health crises like an acute PE can lead to emotional distress, which may manifest as anxiety, anger, depression, or post-traumatic stress disorder. In individuals with chronic heart failure and pulmonary artery hypertension, a diminished quality of life has been linked to poorer prognosis and has become a key focus in treatment strategies for chronic heart failure [[51](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF51)].

The long-term survival impact is significant, particularly for those who develop CTEPH or experience complications such as chronic right heart failure. Predictors of adverse outcomes include residual pulmonary hypertension, severe RV dysfunction, and comorbid conditions such as heart failure or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease [[52](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303#REF52)]. Advanced age, persistent symptoms despite treatment, and non-adherence to therapeutic regimens further exacerbate the risk of poor prognosis and recurrence. Identifying these risk factors is crucial for tailoring individualized treatment plans, implementing preventive measures, and improving long-term patient outcomes. ## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11443303)Conclusions

Recent advancements in the management of PE and RVD are reshaping clinical practice. Prompt diagnosis, effective anticoagulation, and timely interventions are essential for enhancing patient outcomes. Innovations such as targeted anticoagulants, advanced interventional techniques, and personalized medicine offer the potential for more precise treatment strategies. To fully leverage these advancements, it is important to integrate novel therapies with individualized management approaches. Future research should prioritize evaluating the long-term efficacy of new treatments, refining personalized care, and optimizing management protocols to further improve patient outcomes.

results.content: In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), catheter-directed embolectomy is commonly performed but has not been compared with anticoagulation alone. In a recent randomized trial of 100 such patients, suction embolectomy followed by anticoagulation did not improve mortality but did result in a greater reduction of the right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio (an indicator of RV strain) compared with anticoagulation alone (0.52 versus 0.24) . In addition, normalization of tachycardia and indicators of pulmonary artery obstruction improved in a larger proportion of patients undergoing embolectomy. The adverse event rate (including bleeding) was similar between the groups, as was the need [...] AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

What's new in emergency medicine

Authors:[Michael Ganetsky, MD](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)[Jonathan S Grayzel, MD](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)[James F Wiley, II, MD, MPH](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/contributors)

All topics are updated as new evidence becomes available and our [peer review process](https://www.uptodate.com/home/editorial-policy) is complete.

Please read the [Disclaimer](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/8365/print#disclaimerContent)at the end of this page.

The following represent additions to UpToDate from the past six months that were considered by the editors and authors to be of particular interest. The most recent What's New entries are at the top of each subsection.

ADULT RESUSCITATION

Catheter-directed thrombolysis versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), limited data suggest that catheter-directed thrombolysis improves RV function compared with anticoagulation alone, but does not improve mortality. In a recent randomized trial of 544 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE, ultrasound-facilitated, catheter-directed thrombolysis with [alteplase](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/alteplase-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) reduced the composite outcome of PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation, or symptomatic PE recurrence compared with anticoagulation alone (4 versus 10 percent); this difference was driven primarily by fewer episodes of decompensation (3.7 versus 10.3 percent) [[1](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/1)]. Major bleeding was numerically higher in the alteplase group (4 versus 2 percent) but was not statistically significant, and the difference in RV size at 48 hours between the two groups was also not significant. Interpretation is limited by low event rates, lack of blinding, and underrepresentation of patients >75 years. However, these data support our practice of performing catheter-directed therapies in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Catheter-directed thrombolysis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Catheter-directed+thrombolysis&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4140125415&source=see_link#H4140125415).)

Updated international Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (March 2026)

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines have recently been updated [[2](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/2)]. The guidelines suggested that, while a mean arterial pressure of 65 mmHg should be targeted, a range of 60 to 70 mmHg is practical for most adults with sepsis. The guidelines also emphasized the importance of screening tools for early detection and management of sepsis, while discouraging both overly aggressive fluid resuscitation and empiric treatment for fungal and anaerobic bacterial infections, especially when suspicion is low. The guidelines encouraged active fluid removal (in the later phases of shock), rapid de-escalation of antimicrobials and, in mechanically ventilated patients, the use of selective digestive tract decontamination to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia. We agree with these recommendations. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Introduction'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=INTRODUCTION&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1&source=see_link#H1).)

Joint European and United States definition of refractory septic shock (March 2026)

Although sepsis and septic shock have widely accepted definitions, there has not been consensus regarding the definition of "refractory" septic shock. The Society of Critical Care Medicine and European Society of Intensive Care Medicine have recently proposed criteria defining refractory septic shock by the presence of (1) persistently elevated lactate concentration (>2 mmol/L [>18 mg/dL]) and/or prolonged capillary refill time, (2) lack of response to fluid resuscitation, (3) a norepinephrine base equivalent dose >0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute, and (4) in those with suspected mixed shock, critical care ultrasound should be used to confirm lack of response to fluids and to exclude other etiologies for shock [[3](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/3)]. The impact of this definition on patient outcomes, such as survival, remains undetermined. (See ["Sepsis syndromes in adults: Epidemiology, definitions, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and prognosis", section on 'Septic shock'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-syndromes-in-adults-epidemiology-definitions-clinical-presentation-diagnosis-and-prognosis?sectionName=Septic+shock&topicRef=8365&anchor=H8&source=see_link#H8).)

High-flow oxygen does not affect mortality in hypoxemic respiratory failure (March 2026)

Although frequently used, the value of high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure remains unclear. In a randomized trial of 1110 such patients, HFNC did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with low-flow oxygen [[4](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/4)]. HFNC led to a non-significant reduction in the intubation rate at 28 days (42.4 versus 48.4 percent), and rapidly improved patients' respiratory rates, dyspnea, and carbon dioxide levels. These data support our practice of administering HFNC only to patients with advanced oxygen needs (eg, >6 L/minute) rather than routine administration. (See ["Evaluation and management of the nonventilated, hospitalized adult patient with acute hypoxemia", section on 'Humidified, high-flow oxygen delivered via nasal cannulae (HFNC)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-the-nonventilated-hospitalized-adult-patient-with-acute-hypoxemia?sectionName=Humidified%2C+high-flow+oxygen+delivered+via+nasal+cannulae+%28HFNC%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3611214250&source=see_link#H3611214250).)

Updated resuscitation guidelines for adults (January 2026)

The American Heart Association and European Resuscitation Council have published updated guidelines for adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation and emergency care [[5,6](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/5,6)]. Resuscitation updates include: urgent electrical cardioversion for patients who are unstable and those with rate-related ischemia caused by atrial fibrillation or flutter; immediate defibrillation for all adult patients with sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; and increased support for using extracorporeal devices for potentially reversible causes of cardiac arrest where resources are available. Post-resuscitation updates include a normocapnic ventilation target and recommendations for a target temperature ≤37.5°C for a minimum of 36 hours following return of spontaneous circulation. (See ["Advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) in adults", section on 'Management of specific arrhythmias'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/advanced-cardiac-life-support-acls-in-adults?sectionName=MANAGEMENT+OF+SPECIFIC+ARRHYTHMIAS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H7&source=see_link#H7) and ["Intensive care unit management of the intubated post-cardiac arrest adult patient", section on 'Setting the target temperature'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intensive-care-unit-management-of-the-intubated-post-cardiac-arrest-adult-patient?sectionName=Setting+the+target+temperature&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1286775785&source=see_link#H1286775785).)

Induction and tracheal intubation in critically ill patients using etomidate or ketamine (December 2025)

Concern exists regarding induction with [etomidate](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/etomidate-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) during rapid sequence intubation (RSI) in critically ill patients, particularly septic patients, because of transient adrenocortical suppression that may worsen outcomes. [Ketamine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ketamine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) has been proposed as an alternative for such patients, but it stimulates catecholamine release and may increase risk of myocardial ischemia or pulmonary hypertension. A pragmatic trial of more than 2300 critically ill adults undergoing RSI in the emergency department or intensive care unit found similar in-hospital 28-day mortality between the ketamine and etomidate groups (28 versus 29 percent) [[7](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/7)]. Almost half of the patients had sepsis or septic shock, also with no difference in mortality (39 versus 38 percent). These findings suggest that either etomidate or ketamine is a reasonable induction agent in critically ill patients, including those with sepsis. (See ["General anesthesia: Intravenous induction agents", section on 'Disadvantages and adverse effects'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/general-anesthesia-intravenous-induction-agents?sectionName=Disadvantages+and+adverse+effects&topicRef=8365&anchor=H262499028&source=see_link#H262499028).)

Updated sequential organ failure assessment score (SOFA-2) (December 2025)

An updated Sepsis Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, termed SOFA-2, has been published [[8](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/8)]. SOFA-2 resolves many of the deficiencies of SOFA-1 (eg, inclusion of a broader range of organ failure thresholds in the original six organ domains). Data from over 2 million patients in over 1300 intensive care units (ICUs) were used to develop and validate the score in all-comer ICU patients. SOFA-2 and SOFA-1 demonstrated a similar ability to predict ICU mortality. A 1-point increase in SOFA-2 increased the odds of ICU mortality (odds ratio, 1.378). Sequential SOFA-2 calculations from ICU day 1 to 7 remained predictive throughout those seven days. We agree with the updated version of SOFA; however, it does not automatically change the SOFA-1-based Sepsis-3 definition for sepsis and septic shock. (See ["Predictive scoring systems in the intensive care unit", section on 'Sequential (sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/predictive-scoring-systems-in-the-intensive-care-unit?sectionName=Sequential+%28sepsis-related%29+Organ+Failure+Assessment+%28SOFA%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H889841588&source=see_link#H889841588).)

Arterial catheter in shock (December 2025)

Whether an arterial catheter should be routinely inserted in patients with shock is unclear. A recent trial reported outcomes comparing arterial catheter placement with no catheter in over 1000 patients with shock, half of whom had sepsis [[9](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/9)]. Ninety-day mortality was similar between the two groups (34 versus 37 percent). Pain, hemorrhage, and hematoma were more common in the arterial catheter group. Limitations of the study include a lack of blinding, baseline group differences, and limited applicability to specific types of shock. Nonetheless, these results suggest that many patients can be managed without an arterial catheter, although our approach is to place an arterial catheter when a reasonable indication is present (eg, labile blood pressure, unreliable blood pressure readings). (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Monitoring catheters'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=Monitoring+catheters&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3514478798&source=see_link#H3514478798).)

Capillary refill time as a tissue perfusion biomarker in septic shock (December 2025)

Preliminary data suggest that using capillary refill time (CRT) as a clinical biomarker of tissue perfusion may lower mortality in patients with septic shock. In a recent trial, a protocol that used CRT to tailor fluid, vasopressor, and inotrope therapy was compared with usual care in over 1500 patients with early septic shock [[10](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/10)]. The CRT protocol reduced the duration of vital organ support by 5 percent. The CRT group also received less fluid and had a higher percentage of patients receiving vasopressor therapy. However, mortality was similar, the trial was unblinded, and the impact of the additional components of the CRT protocol on outcomes was not accurately assessed. Nonetheless, these data support our practice of including CRT as part of the bedside assessment when monitoring the response to therapy in patients with septic shock. (See ["Evaluation and management of suspected sepsis and septic shock in adults", section on 'Clinical'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-management-of-suspected-sepsis-and-septic-shock-in-adults?sectionName=Clinical&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1643153952&source=see_link#H1643153952).)

Tracheoarterial fistula: A large series description (December 2025)

Tracheoarterial fistula is a late, life-threatening complication of tracheostomy placement associated with high mortality. In a series date of almost 150 patients, the median time to fistula development was 80 days [[11](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/11)]. Only half of patients had the classic feature of an initial small "sentinel" bleed followed by massive hemorrhage a few hours or days later. Imaging (typically computed tomography) was better at diagnosing the fistula than bronchoscopy (80 versus 32 percent). Tracheostomy cuff overinflation and sternal notch pressure controlled the bleeding in over 70 percent of patients while waiting for definitive therapy (ie, endovascular or surgical repair). These data inform early recognition, diagnosis, and treatment of the most fatal complication of tracheostomy. (See ["Tracheostomy: Postoperative care, maintenance, and complications in adults", section on 'Tracheoarterial fistula'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/tracheostomy-postoperative-care-maintenance-and-complications-in-adults?sectionName=Tracheoarterial+fistula&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3292466807&source=see_link#H3292466807).)

ENVIRONMENTAL EMERGENCIES

Iloprost for amputation prevention in frostbite (May 2026)

[Iloprost](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/iloprost-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is a prostacyclin analog that is indicated for the treatment of grade 3 or 4 frostbite (ie, cyanosis that extends proximal to the distal phalanx after rewarming), but supporting evidence is limited. In a study with over 250 patients (80 receiving iloprost) in two Canadian regions that differed in routine iloprost use but with a standardized frostbite care pathway, iloprost was associated with a lower amputation rate for grade 3 frostbite (30 versus 53 percent) but not for grade 2 and 4 frostbite; patients receiving a higher total iloprost dose were less likely to have amputations [[12](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/12)]. In 40 patients with grade 4 frostbite, iloprost treatment was associated with fewer finger and toe segment amputations (40 versus 51 percent and 47 versus 58 percent, respectively). These findings support our recommendation for iloprost in patients with severe frostbite. (See ["Frostbite: Acute care and prevention", section on 'Iloprost within 72 hours'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/frostbite-acute-care-and-prevention?sectionName=Iloprost+within+72+hours&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1902794625&source=see_link#H1902794625).)

Microorganisms in children with freshwater drowning-associated pneumonia (February 2026)

Infection with gram-negative organisms, especially _Aeromonas_ species, is predominantly reported in patients with drowning-associated pneumonia (DAP). In a study from China of over 70 children with freshwater DAP in a pediatric intensive care unit, _Staphylococcus aureus_ was the most isolated organism [[13](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/13)]. Other common pathogens included _Mycoplasma pneumoniae_, _Streptococcus pneumoniae_, _Haemophilus influenzae_, _Klebsiella pneumoniae_, _Candida albicans_, and rhinovirus. These findings highlight the need for an empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic regimen, including coverage of gram-positive bacteria, in children with suspected DAP. (See ["Drowning (submersion injuries)", section on 'Pneumonia'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/drowning-submersion-injuries?sectionName=Pneumonia&topicRef=8365&anchor=H809358478&source=see_link#H809358478).)

Effectiveness of defibrillation in patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable rhythm (February 2026)

Patients with hypothermia and nonperfusing shockable arrhythmias are less likely to have return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with defibrillation at a core temperature <30°C (86°F). Current recommendations are to attempt defibrillation with up to three shocks but withhold further attempts pending rewarming since cold myocardium can potentially be injured. A registry-based study with almost 40 patients with cardiac arrest, a shockable rhythm, and core temperature <30°C found that ROSC was more likely if defibrillation was performed during rewarming, as compared with before rewarming (100 versus 25 percent) [[14](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/14)]. Defibrillation during extracorporeal life support (ECLS) had a fivefold increase in odds of ROSC. These findings support our recommendations to attempt defibrillation even with temperature <30°C and to not withhold defibrillation during ECLS rewarming at temperature >25°C (77°F). (See ["Accidental hypothermia in adults: Management", section on 'Ventricular arrhythmias or asystole'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/accidental-hypothermia-in-adults-management?sectionName=Ventricular+arrhythmias+or+asystole&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1808505299&source=see_link#H1808505299).)

Acute hypersensitivity reactions from rattlesnake antivenom in alpha-gal endemic region (February 2026)

CroFab and Anavip, antivenoms used to treat Crotalinae snakebite envenomation, can potentially cause severe allergic reactions. Anavip contains more of the carbohydrate moiety galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (which is responsible for alpha-gal syndrome) compared with CroFab. A study with over 200 patients in Arkansas (a state with a high rate of alpha-gal sensitization) who received either Anavip or CroFab found that Anavip was associated with increased adverse drug reactions (including presumed anaphylaxis) compared with CroFab (22 versus 4 percent) [[15](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/15)]. Basophil activation testing from individuals with known alpha-gal syndrome found that Anavip more potently activated alpha-gal sensitized basophils. Clinicians who treat snakebite victims in regions with high rates of alpha-gal sensitization must be ready to manage anaphylaxis following antivenom (especially Anavip) administration. (See ["Bites by Crotalinae snakes (rattlesnakes, cottonmouths [water moccasins], or copperheads) in the United States: Management", section on 'Acute antivenom hypersensitivity reactions'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/bites-by-crotalinae-snakes-rattlesnakes-cottonmouths-water-moccasins-or-copperheads-in-the-united-states-management?sectionName=Acute+antivenom+hypersensitivity+reactions&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4098260420&source=see_link#H4098260420).)

GENERAL ADULT EMERGENCY MEDICINE

Fosphenytoin for trigeminal neuralgia attacks (May 2026)

Several pharmacologic options are available to treat acute trigeminal neuralgia (TN) pain, but available supporting evidence is limited. In a randomized trial that included 22 patients with acute TN symptoms, pain reduction on the numerical rating scale (0 for no pain up to 10 for worst pain) was greater at two hours among those assigned to [fosphenytoin](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fosphenytoin-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) than placebo (-6.1 versus -2.4) [[16](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/16)]. Treatment consisted of a loading dose followed by once daily maintenance treatment for up to four days. Patients assigned to fosphenytoin also had a higher rate of >50 percent pain reduction and reduction in the frequency of attack recurrence, and treatment was generally well tolerated. These data provide clinical trial evidence to support the role of fosphenytoin for acute TN exacerbations. (See ["Trigeminal neuralgia", section on 'Acute rescue therapy for patients with breakthrough pain'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/trigeminal-neuralgia?sectionName=Acute+rescue+therapy+for+patients+with+breakthrough+pain&topicRef=8365&anchor=H372586115&source=see_link#H372586115).)

AHA/ACC guidelines for pulmonary embolism (March 2026)

Several societies, including the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC), have issued joint guidelines for the evaluation and management of pulmonary embolism (PE) [[17](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/17)]. The guidelines stratify patients by risk of PE-related death to facilitate management. Patients in category A (incidental PE), B (symptomatic PE with a low clinical severity score), and C (symptomatic PE with an elevated clinical severity score) require anticoagulation. Patients in category D (incipient cardiopulmonary failure) and E (cardiopulmonary failure) are candidates for reperfusion therapies (eg, thrombectomy or thrombolysis, if they have a low bleeding risk). We await adoption of this classification and encourage its use to facilitate management. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Treatment overview and prognosis", section on 'American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology/others'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-treatment-overview-and-prognosis?sectionName=American+Heart+Association%2FAmerican+College+of+Cardiology%2Fothers&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2148862999&source=see_link#H2148862999).)

Age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs in deep vein thrombosis diagnosis (January 2026)

D-dimer values rise with age, decreasing specificity in older patients when a fixed cutoff is used to diagnose deep venous thrombosis (DVT). In a study of 2169 patients with low to moderate pretest probability for DVT, using an age-adjusted D-dimer (age [years] x 10 ng/mL for patients >50 years) compared with a fixed conventional cutoff of 500 ng/mL resulted in a 7 percent absolute increase in patients for whom DVT was excluded without lower extremity compression ultrasonography [[18](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/18)]. At three months, there were no VTE events in patients with a D-dimer level ≥500 ng/mL but below the age-adjusted cutoff. These data strengthen the case for more widespread utilization of age-adjusted D-dimer to diagnose DVT in older adults. (See ["Clinical presentation and diagnosis of the nonpregnant adult with suspected deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremity", section on 'Adjusted cutoffs'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/clinical-presentation-and-diagnosis-of-the-nonpregnant-adult-with-suspected-deep-vein-thrombosis-of-the-lower-extremity?sectionName=Adjusted+cutoffs&topicRef=8365&anchor=H410968138&source=see_link#H410968138).)

Andexanet alfa removed from the United States market (January 2026)

[Andexanet alfa](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/andexanet-alfa-inactivated-coagulation-factor-xa-recombinant-united-states-withdrawn-from-market-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), a specific reversal agent for factor Xa inhibitors that was approved in 2018, has been removed from the United States market, as reported in a communication from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) [[19](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/19)]. The communication mentions concerns about an increased rate of serious thrombotic complications compared with usual care in the ANNEXA-I trial and states that the company has voluntarily withdrawn the licensing application for commercial reasons. For life-threatening bleeding associated with factor Xa inhibitors, 4-factor unactivated prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) can be used along with other hemostatic measures. (See ["Management of bleeding in patients receiving direct oral anticoagulants", section on 'Andexanet alfa'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/management-of-bleeding-in-patients-receiving-direct-oral-anticoagulants?sectionName=Andexanet+alfa&topicRef=8365&anchor=H635532401&source=see_link#H635532401) and ["Hemostatic treatments for anticoagulated patients with intracranial hemorrhage", section on 'Andexanet alfa if PCC is unavailable'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/hemostatic-treatments-for-anticoagulated-patients-with-intracranial-hemorrhage?sectionName=Andexanet+alfa+if+PCC+is+unavailable&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4272016095&source=see_link#H4272016095).)

Suction embolectomy versus anticoagulation in pulmonary embolism (January 2026)

In patients with intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (PE; ie, biochemical and imaging evidence of right ventricle [RV] dysfunction), catheter-directed embolectomy is commonly performed but has not been compared with anticoagulation alone. In a recent randomized trial of 100 such patients, suction embolectomy followed by anticoagulation did not improve mortality but did result in a greater reduction of the right ventricular (RV)/left ventricular (LV) ratio (an indicator of RV strain) compared with anticoagulation alone (0.52 versus 0.24) [[20](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/20)]. In addition, normalization of tachycardia and indicators of pulmonary artery obstruction improved in a larger proportion of patients undergoing embolectomy. The adverse event rate (including bleeding) was similar between the groups, as was the need for intensive care unit admission and hospital length of stay; PE did not recur in either group. This study provides additional support for the use of catheter-directed embolectomy in patients with intermediate-high-risk PE with the goal of faster thrombus resolution and reduction in RV load. (See ["Acute pulmonary embolism in adults: Reperfusion therapy in intermediate- and high-risk patients", section on 'Suction/mechanical embolectomy'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-pulmonary-embolism-in-adults-reperfusion-therapy-in-intermediate-and-high-risk-patients?sectionName=Suction%2Fmechanical+embolectomy&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3973928105&source=see_link#H3973928105).)

Post-thoracentesis ultrasonography for residual fluid evaluation (December 2025)

With the routine use of lung ultrasonography for therapeutic thoracentesis, it is unclear whether post-procedure chest radiography to still necessary to assess for residual fluid. In a recent prospective study of 147 patients with a free-flowing pleural effusion, there was excellent agreement between lung ultrasonography (performed immediately after the procedure) and chest radiography (performed four hours after thoracentesis; Gwet's agreement coefficient 0.93) [[21](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/21)]. There was also strong agreement between the proceduralist's interpretation and that of the blind ultrasound reviewer (kappa 0.81). These results suggest that ultrasonography is sufficient for evaluating residual fluid after thoracentesis; however, these findings may not be generalizable to patients with trapped lung and need additional study. (See ["Ultrasound-guided thoracentesis", section on 'Follow-up'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ultrasound-guided-thoracentesis?sectionName=FOLLOW-UP&topicRef=8365&anchor=H9&source=see_link#H9).)

Pediatric sepsis hospitalization and mortality in the United States (March 2026)

New estimates of United States sepsis hospitalizations and in-hospital mortality based on a pediatric sepsis event definition derived from the 2024 Phoenix sepsis criteria have been reported using electronic-health record surveillance of clinical data from over 3.9 million pediatric hospitalizations (neonates excluded) from 2016 to 2023. The average annual hospital incidence of sepsis was 1.3 percent (over 18,000 annual cases); overall in-hospital mortality was 10.1 percent (over 1800 annual deaths) [[22,23](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/22,23)]. Annualized national estimates remained stable over the study period. These findings update prior sepsis estimates based upon older definitions of pediatric sepsis and confirm the high burden of pediatric illness due to sepsis in the United States. (See ["Sepsis in children: Definitions, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Burden of disease'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sepsis-in-children-definitions-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Burden+of+disease&topicRef=8365&anchor=H632992306&source=see_link#H632992306).)

Ibuprofen for acute pediatric musculoskeletal injuries (January 2026)

Most experts recommend nonopioid medications as first-line therapy for acute pain in children. However, for children with acute musculoskeletal injuries (eg, fractures and sprains), some clinicians and caregivers have concerns that pain could be undertreated without opioids. A recent trial randomly assigned nearly 700 children with nonoperative musculoskeletal extremity injuries (primarily nondisplaced fractures and sprains) and moderate pain to [ibuprofen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/ibuprofen-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) alone, ibuprofen plus [acetaminophen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acetaminophen-paracetamol-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), or ibuprofen plus an oral opioid ([hydromorphone](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/hydromorphone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) [[24](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/24)]. Ibuprofen alone provided similar analgesia as the combined analgesia strategies and was associated with fewer adverse effects compared with ibuprofen plus hydromorphone. These findings confirm that nonopioid medications alone are sufficient for most children with acute musculoskeletal pain, and the addition of an opioid only increases the risk of adverse events. (See ["Pain in children: Approach to pain assessment and overview of management principles", section on 'Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pain-in-children-approach-to-pain-assessment-and-overview-of-management-principles?sectionName=Nonsteroidal+anti-inflammatory+drugs&topicRef=8365&anchor=H15&source=see_link#H15).)

Lumbar puncture in low-risk febrile neonates (December 2025)

Current guidelines advise lumbar puncture (LP) to evaluate for meningitis in all febrile neonates seen in the outpatient setting, with an option to omit LP in selected patients 22 to 28 days old at low risk. In a new meta-analysis of four prospective cohort studies (1537 previously healthy febrile, full-term neonates <28 days old [meningitis prevalence 0.7 percent]), of the 632 patients identified as low risk for invasive bacterial infection by the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) rule, none had meningitis (negative predictive value 99.96 percent) [[25](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/25)]. These findings suggest that it may be reasonable to omit LP in selected febrile neonates after shared decision-making with parents/primary caregivers as long as they are managed by experienced physicians and other clinicians in facilities with adequate resources to closely and safely monitor neonates. However, LP is still necessary in the majority of febrile neonates ≥7 days old. (See ["The febrile neonate (28 days of age or younger): Outpatient evaluation", section on '7 to 21 days old'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/the-febrile-neonate-28-days-of-age-or-younger-outpatient-evaluation?sectionName=7+to+21+days+old&topicRef=8365&anchor=H857933794&source=see_link#H857933794).)

Botulism associated with contaminated or unlicensed products (December 2025)

Although botulism is uncommon in the United States, recent cases have highlighted the risk of contaminated or unlicensed products. Between August and November 2025, 37 cases of infant botulism were linked to a particular brand of powdered formula (ByHeart) [[26](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/26)]; the causative organism, _Clostridium botulinum,_ was detected in several formula samples and all products from this brand were recalled. In addition, three unrelated cases of iatrogenic botulism were reported following self-injection of unlicensed botulinum toxin products purchased from various online vendors in Asia [[27](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/27)]. Clinicians should consider the possibility of botulism and evaluate for potential exposures in infants with acute onset of weak suck, ptosis, hypotonia, and/or constipation and in older individuals with features of acute cranial neuropathy (eg, ptosis, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia) and limb weakness, particularly if fever is absent. (See ["Botulism", section on 'Forms of botulism and their sources'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/botulism?sectionName=FORMS+OF+BOTULISM+AND+THEIR+SOURCES&topicRef=8365&anchor=H6&source=see_link#H6) and ["Neuromuscular junction disorders in newborns and infants", section on 'Infant botulism'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/neuromuscular-junction-disorders-in-newborns-and-infants?sectionName=INFANT+BOTULISM&topicRef=8365&anchor=H14&source=see_link#H14).)

Rapid analgesia for sickle cell pain in the ED (November 2025)

Most individuals with sickle cell disease (SCD)-associated pain only present to the emergency department (ED) or day hospital when their pain has exceeded what they can manage at home. In a new study involving over 2500 children with SCD who presented to the ED with pain, receiving the first dose of an opioid within 60 minutes of arrival was much less likely to be associated with inpatient hospitalization, and receiving the second dose within 30 minutes after the first further reduced hospitalization risk [[28](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/28)]. Many children in this study received intranasal [fentanyl](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), which correlated with faster time to first opioid dose. This study provides concrete evidence of how impactful rapid analgesia can be for individuals with SCD. (See ["Acute vaso-occlusive pain management in sickle cell disease (children and adults)", section on 'Give pain medication promptly (within 60 minutes)'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-vaso-occlusive-pain-management-in-sickle-cell-disease-children-and-adults?sectionName=Give+pain+medication+promptly+%28within+60+minutes%29&topicRef=8365&anchor=H916987485&source=see_link#H916987485).)
