International guidelines for the management of pediatric sepsis and septic shock (May 2026)

The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Pediatric Guidelines for the management of sepsis and septic shock in children are available [[29](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/29)]. The guidelines reaffirm the prime importance of the rapid recognition of septic shock and treatment that includes timely administration of fluid bolus therapy, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and, in patients not responding to fluid bolus therapy, initiation of vasoactive medications (epinephrine or norepinephrine) ([algorithm 1](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)). The 2026 guidelines also provide new recommendations that promote the use of blood lactate trends, lung and cardiac point-of-care ultrasound, and central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO 2 ≥ 70 percent) to monitor resuscitation. Our approach is consistent with these guidelines. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Approach'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Approach&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2493912177&source=see_link#H2493912177).)

Balanced crystalloid solution versus normal saline for children with septic shock (April 2026)

For children with septic shock, whether to administer balanced crystalloid solutions (BCS; for example, [lactated Ringer](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/lactated-ringer-solution-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)'s) versus normal [saline](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/sodium-chloride-preparations-saline-and-oral-salt-tablets-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (NS) during initial fluid resuscitation is unclear. In a new randomized trial of over 8400 children with suspected septic shock, the combined outcomes of death, initiation of renal-replacement therapy, and persistent kidney dysfunction at 30 days were not significantly different in patients who were assigned to fluid resuscitation for up to 48 hours with BCS (3.4 percent) versus NS (3 percent) [[30](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/30)]. Hyperchloremia and hypernatremia were more common in patients receiving NS; increased blood lactate was more common in patients receiving BCS. Otherwise, adverse effects were similar in both groups. These findings suggest that either BCS or NS is an appropriate choice for fluid resuscitation of children with septic shock. However, the results may not be generalizable to patients with hospital-acquired sepsis or those treated in resource-limited settings. (See ["Children with sepsis in resource-abundant settings: Rapid recognition and initial resuscitation (first hour)", section on 'Fluid resuscitation'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/children-with-sepsis-in-resource-abundant-settings-rapid-recognition-and-initial-resuscitation-first-hour?sectionName=Fluid+resuscitation&topicRef=8365&anchor=H19450206&source=see_link#H19450206).)

2025 neonatal resuscitation guidelines (January 2026)

The American Heart Association/American Academy of Pediatrics/International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation/European Resuscitation Council (AHA/AAP/ILCOR/ERC) have published updated guidelines for neonatal resuscitation [[31-33](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/31-33)]. The guidelines reaffirm the previously published guidelines and neonatal resuscitative algorithm ([algorithm 2](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)). Modifications include updated recommendations for oxygen concentrations during initial resuscitation of preterm neonates (21 to 30 percent if 32 to <35 weeks of gestation, ≥30 percent if <32 weeks of gestation to achieve target oxygen saturation goals); initial peak inflation pressures (20 to 25 cm H 2 O if <32 weeks of gestation, 25 to 30 cm H 2 O if ≥32 weeks of gestation); measurement of endotracheal tube (ETT) insertion depth from tip to upper gum instead of tip to lip; and smaller ETT sizes for premature/low birth weight neonates. (See ["Neonatal resuscitation in the delivery room", section on 'Overview of approach'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/neonatal-resuscitation-in-the-delivery-room?sectionName=Overview+of+approach&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2429918249&source=see_link#H2429918249).)

2025 pediatric advanced life support and basic life support guidelines (December 2025)

The American Heart Association (AHA) and the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) have published updated guidelines for Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) and Basic Life Support (BLS). The PALS guidelines reaffirm the emergency management of children with [bradycardia](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-Bradycardia-250121.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=q1pyrfBCbwFQJhc%2FMhbXjoDdj37GKNcvBArRruz4pi6prBWUwv9beMvsqP%2FK2xAfbvK884G79KE6fdnFMRXMM4fZAcZ5TzU5KFZrr6%2B23CknCjswgsstcbNI3gFKwwenEkwPM2igGHKUxJXjffIQ8On7WMAqa%2BQE8j%2BSsDFvZM4%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365), [tachycardia](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-Tachyarrhythmia-250117.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=bMVDu3EwdQxRH00JMQHDLRQwGh1cclKlOyJ0Sl09whnFFbUzXKhrVbaEd0twQsKDKZjLqxYL5bwFayuhT%2FmkzZ0d%2FE6OdY%2F3%2BgP5rQmOblEgtT9hTOIra%2F%2Bln2i5svyPWGqh95oZeYA7moAvA%2FOIk%2BltqJ183iDuQJnlXkoVZgg%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365), and [pulseless arrest](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FAlgorithm-PALS-CA-250123.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=1lOXrl%2BAUwYFmmQHMw%2BxoR268snn0ENhenLHVT3D6c4bcZBFrNH%2F1HzPV2NrM9tbTMnz%2F0fSV%2B5hrAopPfQH6oKx9IyimzNo6fX%2BOAopVjZKTuKmCoo8d7Kpsf91LV9EHBS7jb49W6DIr7zXUYKCNA%3D%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365). During cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), PALS advises end-tidal CO 2 monitoring when feasible and new diastolic blood pressure goals of 25 mmHg in infants and ≥30 mmHg in children when invasive arterial monitoring is available [[34](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/34)]. Important changes to the pediatric BLS [guidance](https://www.uptodate.com/external-redirect?target_url=https%3A%2F%2Fcpr.heart.org%2F-%2Fmedia%2FCPR-Files%2FCPR-Guidelines-Files%2F2025-Algorithms%2FFigure-10-Pediatric-BLS-Algorithm-2-or-more-Rescuers.pdf%3Fsc_lang%3Den&token=b0aL%2FnN446ptMOOUoUchsjAVkGAnJoJSFCzpYBbuTOw7bTBt%2F7EnUJBbs8aoceEvBMuSYIFfIOZL%2BqZZA6yLwPasi9oeyYlUfTQ3nOV5z7FlWi1YmCy5L5yFJYzKjlfzA%2BR92e7gaavzgGcH9HppR%2FGPazKDGT3FWu5cmydfre4%3D&TOPIC_ID=8365)include new recommendations for the heel-of-one-hand or the thumb-encircling technique when performing cardiac compressions in infants (the two-finger technique is **not**recommended) and administration of [naloxone](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/naloxone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) during CPR when an opioid overdose is suspected [[35](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/35)]. We agree with these guidelines. (See ["Pediatric advanced life support (PALS)", section on 'AHA resuscitation guidelines'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pediatric-advanced-life-support-pals?sectionName=AHA+RESUSCITATION+GUIDELINES&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3969530922&source=see_link#H3969530922) and ["Pediatric basic life support (BLS) for health care providers", section on 'Infants'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pediatric-basic-life-support-bls-for-health-care-providers?sectionName=Infants&topicRef=8365&anchor=H9&source=see_link#H9) and ["Pediatric basic life support (BLS) for health care providers", section on 'Basic life support approach'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/pediatric-basic-life-support-bls-for-health-care-providers?sectionName=BASIC+LIFE+SUPPORT+APPROACH&topicRef=8365&anchor=H4&source=see_link#H4)pproach'.)

PRIMARY CARE ORTHOPEDICS AND SPORTS MEDICINE

Management of severely displaced distal radius fractures in children (April 2026)

For children with severely displaced distal radius fractures, the usual approach is fracture reduction and casting by a clinician or orthopedic surgeon with pediatric expertise. In a pragmatic trial of 750 children (4 to 10 years old) with severely displaced distal radial fractures, patients with markedly displaced Salter-Harris I or II physeal or metaphyseal fractures, were randomized to surgical reduction and casting versus casting alone [[36](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/36)]. At three months, functional outcomes, pain, and quality of life measured by validated scores as well as subjective cosmesis were significantly better in the surgical group. However, the difference in scores was small and less than minimally important differences for each outcome and became nonsignificant along with cosmesis at 12 months. These findings suggest that casting alone by an experienced clinician or orthopedic surgeon may be a reasonable option in children <10 years old with these injuries. However, we continue to support prompt reduction and casting pending further confirmation of these results. (See ["Distal forearm fractures in children: Initial management", section on 'Complete fracture'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/distal-forearm-fractures-in-children-initial-management?sectionName=Complete+fracture&topicRef=8365&anchor=H34&source=see_link#H34) and ["Distal forearm fractures in children: Initial management", section on 'Displaced Salter-Harris I or II fractures'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/distal-forearm-fractures-in-children-initial-management?sectionName=Displaced+Salter-Harris+I+or+II+fractures&topicRef=8365&anchor=H26&source=see_link#H26).)

Persistent symptoms of concussion in young children (March 2026)

In a prospective study, 235 young children (median age 2.4 years, 98 percent with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15) were diagnosed with concussion in the emergency department (ED) based on the GCS score and ≥1 of the following: palpable skull fracture, headache (in verbal patients), altered mental status, or loss of consciousness [[37](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/37)]. At one month, 28 percent had persistent symptoms on a parent-reported symptoms score. This rate was significantly higher than in controls with orthopedic injuries undergoing ED evaluation and community children. On adjusted analysis, ED symptom severity was the primary predictor of persistent symptoms. These findings suggest that, similar to older children and adolescents, young children appear to have a significant risk of persistent symptoms of concussion after a mild head injury that appears to be associated with the severity of symptoms at initial evaluation. (See ["Concussion in children and adolescents: Management", section on 'Prognosis'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/concussion-in-children-and-adolescents-management?sectionName=PROGNOSIS&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2832537&source=see_link#H2832537).)

Management of displaced medial epicondyle elbow fractures in children (January 2026)

For children with medial epicondyle elbow fractures, the degree of displacement that warrants operative intervention is debated. A multicenter pragmatic trial of 334 children with these fractures (24 percent with associated reducible elbow dislocations) randomly assigned patients to immobilization (typically cast or splinting) versus surgical treatment [[38](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/38)]. At 12 months after injury, functional outcomes, participation in sports and performing arts, pain, and quality of life were similar in the two groups; children assigned to surgery had more complications. These findings suggest that nonsurgical treatment is appropriate for most children with closed, displaced medial epicondyle elbow fractures. Surgical repair is still necessary for selected fractures complicated by an entrapped bony fragment in the elbow joint, ulnar nerve dysfunction, irreducible dislocation, or elbow instability. (See ["Epicondylar and transphyseal elbow fractures in children", section on 'Medial epicondylar fractures'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/epicondylar-and-transphyseal-elbow-fractures-in-children?sectionName=Medial+epicondylar+fractures&topicRef=8365&anchor=H17&source=see_link#H17).)

TOXICOLOGY

Poisoning-related fatality from illicit substances in children and adolescents (May 2026)

Illicit substances such as opioids can result in poisoning-related fatality in pediatric patients. In an analysis conducted on national surveillance databases from the Centers for Disease Control, the rate of death from poisoning (including illicit drug overdoses) in children and adolescents aged 1 to 19 years increased by 12.7 percent from 2020 to 2023 [[39](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/39)]. In 2023, 1913 deaths were from illicit drug overdoses, and the majority (79.5 percent) were from [fentanyl](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link). These findings confirm that illicit substances remain a common cause of fatality in children and adolescents, and that ongoing educational and other preventive measures are warranted in this population. (See ["Poisoning in children: Prevention", section on 'Fatalities'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/poisoning-in-children-prevention?sectionName=Fatalities&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2&source=see_link#H2).)

Poisoning-related injury from ingested household products in young children (May 2026)

Ingested household products remain a common cause of poisoning-related injury in young children. An analysis of national surveillance data estimated that over 240,000 children aged ≤5 years were treated in United States emergency departments for injuries from exposure to household cleaning products from 2007 to 2022 [[40](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/40)]. Approximately 60 percent of injuries were from ingestion. The products and containers associated with the most injuries were bleach (30.1 percent), detergents (28.6 percent), detergent packets (33 percent), and spray bottles (28.2 percent). These findings highlight the importance of ongoing educational, regulatory, and product engineering measures to prevent injuries from ingested substances in pediatric patients. (See ["Poisoning in children: Prevention", section on 'Ingested substances'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/poisoning-in-children-prevention?sectionName=Ingested+substances&topicRef=8365&anchor=H108484245&source=see_link#H108484245).)

Rome V diagnostic criteria for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (April 2026)

Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) is a clinical diagnosis. The Rome V criteria, which update the commonly used Rome IV criteria, were recently published [[41](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/41)]. A patient meets the Rome V criteria for CHS if all of the following are present:

●Stereotypical episodic vomiting resembling cyclic vomiting syndrome in terms of onset, duration, and frequency

●Presentation after prolonged (one year) and excessive cannabis use (≥4 days per week or ≥15 doses per week, or both)

●Relief of vomiting episodes by sustained cessation of cannabis use (at least six months or three typical emetic cycles)

Association with pathologic bathing behavior (prolonged hot baths or showers) is supportive but not necessary. We agree that these criteria can assist in diagnosing CHS. (See ["Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome", section on 'Diagnostic criteria'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/cannabinoid-hyperemesis-syndrome?sectionName=Diagnostic+criteria&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3072534301&source=see_link#H3072534301).)

New recommendations on use of activated charcoal for overdoses (April 2026)

[Activated charcoal](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/activated-charcoal-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (AC) adsorbs chemicals within minutes of contact, preventing gastrointestinal (GI) absorption and subsequent toxicity. Indications and timing are debatable, and "routine" use for GI decontamination has not demonstrated reduced morbidity and mortality in poisoned patients. Newly released recommendations from the Clinical Toxicology Recommendations Collaborative (which included representatives from three toxicology societies) suggest a potential benefit for a slightly prolonged window for AC administration for ingestion of certain agents (eg, [acetaminophen](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acetaminophen-paracetamol-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), salicylates, and [verapamil](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/verapamil-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) and an additional dose of AC for agents with potential for prolonged GI tract persistence (aforementioned agents as well as [carbamazepine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/carbamazepine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), [valproic acid](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/valproate-valproic-acid-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), paraquat, [phenobarbital](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/phenobarbital-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link), and [theophylline](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/theophylline-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link)) [[42](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/42)]. We agree with most of the recommendations from the Collaborative. (See ["Gastrointestinal decontamination of the poisoned patient", section on 'Indications'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/gastrointestinal-decontamination-of-the-poisoned-patient?sectionName=Indications&topicRef=8365&anchor=H18993776&source=see_link#H18993776).)

Trends in kratom exposures reported to United States poison centers (March 2026)

Kratom (_Mitragyna speciosa_) is a natural product derived from a tree native to Southeast Asia used for its stimulant, analgesic, and antidepressant properties. Commercially sold kratom products can have alkaloidal concentrations that are different compared with natural leaf products, which can cause toxicity and dependence. There were over 14,000 kratom exposures reported to United States poison centers between 2015 and 2025 [[43](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/43)]. Reports steadily increased through 2019, plateaued through 2024, and surged in 2025 (over 3400 reported exposures). Reports involving multiple substances (eg, opioids) were more likely to cause serious outcomes and hospitalization. These findings suggest that kratom-related adverse effects are increasing in the United States. (See ["Kratom health effects from acute and chronic use", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/kratom-health-effects-from-acute-and-chronic-use?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2211216297&source=see_link#H2211216297).)

Chronic lead exposure and increased cardiovascular mortality (March 2026)

Cumulative lead exposure has been linked to an increased risk of atherosclerosis, cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality, and all-cause mortality. A study of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 1999 to 2014, including over 42,000 individuals, reported that higher estimated bone lead levels were associated with increased CVD mortality; the group with the greatest lead burden had an 88 percent increase in adjusted mortality risk compared with estimated preindustrial levels [[44](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/44)]. This corresponds to an estimated 3.5 million deaths globally in 2023 attributable to elevated bone lead levels, which would account for almost 6 percent of deaths and would make lead exposure the eighth leading risk for global mortality. These findings highlight the need to screen for and mitigate occupational and environmental lead exposure. (See ["Lead exposure, toxicity, and poisoning in adults: Clinical manifestations and diagnosis", section on 'Chronic and long-term exposure effects'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/lead-exposure-toxicity-and-poisoning-in-adults-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Chronic+and+long-term+exposure+effects&topicRef=8365&anchor=H7&source=see_link#H7).)

Causes and prognosis of acquired methemoglobinemia (March 2026)

Acquired methemoglobinemia is a potentially life-threatening condition in which the iron in heme becomes oxidized and cannot deliver oxygen. In a new study from Thailand that evaluated 169 individuals with acquired methemoglobinemia over a 10-year period, the most common causes were [dapsone](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/dapsone-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (in 30 percent) and the contact herbicide propanil (in 27 percent, mostly for self-harm) [[45](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/45)]. Approximately 10 percent had glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. The fatality rate was 11 percent, 40 percent were admitted to the intensive care unit, 34 percent required intubation, and 89 percent were hospitalized. These data reinforce the importance of rapid recognition and treatment of this condition. (See ["Methemoglobinemia", section on 'Most common acquired causes'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/methemoglobinemia?sectionName=Most+common+acquired+causes&topicRef=8365&anchor=H3113698015&source=see_link#H3113698015).)

Cardiotoxicity of supratherapeutic loperamide exposures (March 2026)

The antidiarrheal agent [loperamide](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/loperamide-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) has been reported to cause ventricular conduction disturbances, including QRS and QT interval prolongation, idioventricular rhythm, and ventricular tachycardia, following overdose. Loperamide is a synthetic opioid but does not typically cause classic signs of opioid toxicity. A systematic review of almost 130 cases of supratherapeutic loperamide exposure found that severe toxicity has been reported at daily doses as low as 20 to 40 mg [[46](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/46)]. Syncope was reported in almost half of cases, while severe cases mainly had polymorphic or sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. These findings suggest that patients with supratherapeutic loperamide exposure may benefit from cardiac monitoring. (See ["Acute opioid intoxication in adults", section on 'Loperamide'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-opioid-intoxication-in-adults?sectionName=Loperamide&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2282453505&source=see_link#H2282453505).)

Psilocybin use in Oregon and Colorado following decriminalization (March 2026)

Psilocybin is a hallucinogen found in many species of mushrooms and has been studied for the treatment of various mental health disorders. Psilocybin was decriminalized for use in licensed clinics in Oregon in 2020 and Colorado in 2022. A study of data from a national survey of drug use from 2018 to 2025 found that self-reported use increased in both states following decriminalization (mean prevalence increased from 2 to 4.5 percent and 2.7 to 4.3 percent in Oregon and Colorado, respectively) [[47](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/47)]. This increase was greater than a weighted composite control of the other states. These findings may impact policy decisions regarding psilocybin decriminalization for therapeutic use. (See ["Intoxication from LSD and other common hallucinogens", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/intoxication-from-lsd-and-other-common-hallucinogens?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H57999532&source=see_link#H57999532).)

Test characteristics of an enzymatic ethylene glycol assay (March 2026)

Ethylene glycol poisoning is potentially fatal if not treated promptly. Diagnosis can be challenging since ethylene glycol concentrations are usually performed by gas chromatography, which is not widely available and typically has long turn-around times. A modification to a glycerol dehydrogenase-based assay approved for veterinary use has been externally validated and is used by some hospitals; it can be performed 24/7 and has a typical turn-around time of several hours. A study of over 400 samples analyzed by both an enzymatic assay and chromatography found a sensitivity and specificity of 89 and 83 percent, respectively [[48](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/48)]. All four false-negative enzymatic results were below the 20 mg/dL treatment threshold. These results suggest that an enzymatic ethylene glycol assay may be a valuable screening tool. (See ["Methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning: Pharmacology, clinical manifestations, and diagnosis", section on 'Testing for methanol and ethylene glycol'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/methanol-and-ethylene-glycol-poisoning-pharmacology-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis?sectionName=Testing+for+methanol+and+ethylene+glycol&topicRef=8365&anchor=H12&source=see_link#H12).)

ED-initiated injectable extended-release buprenorphine (February 2026)

Previous studies have found that emergency department (ED) initiation of sublingual [buprenorphine](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/buprenorphine-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) is associated with decreased all-cause and opioid-related mortality and is feasible and cost-effective. A new trial with almost 2000 ED patients who had untreated opioid use disorder and signs of withdrawal found that ED patients started on extended-release injectable buprenorphine, compared with sublingual buprenorphine, had similar engagement in opioid use disorder treatment at 7 (41 versus 39 percent) and 30 days (44 versus 45 percent) [[49](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/49)]. The rate of precipitated withdrawal was similar and rare (<1 percent) in both groups despite a high prevalence of [fentanyl](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/fentanyl-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) dependence (76 percent). These results suggest that initiation of extended-release injectable buprenorphine may be a safe and feasible option in ED patients for treatment of an opioid use disorder. (See ["Acute opioid intoxication in adults", section on 'Prevention of recurrent opioid overdose'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/acute-opioid-intoxication-in-adults?sectionName=PREVENTION+OF+RECURRENT+OPIOID+OVERDOSE&topicRef=8365&anchor=H10057659&source=see_link#H10057659).)

Impact of arsenic exposure reduction on chronic disease mortality (December 2025)

Chronic exposure to inorganic arsenic has been associated with increased all-cause, cancer, and cardiovascular mortality. Prior studies found population-level improvements in mortality following arsenic mitigation efforts, but individual-level evidence is lacking. An 18-year study that followed almost 11,000 patients in Bangladesh exposed to arsenic in drinking water found a dose-response association between reduced arsenic exposure and lower mortality [[50](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/50)]. Each decrease in the interquartile range of urine arsenic concentration (approximately 200 mcg/g creatinine) was associated with a 22, 20, and 23 percent decrease in chronic disease, cancer, and cardiovascular disease mortality, respectively. These findings support the essential steps in managing chronic arsenic poisoning: identifying the source, mitigating the exposure, and eliminating ongoing and future exposure. (See ["Arsenic exposure and chronic poisoning", section on 'Preventing ongoing exposure'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/arsenic-exposure-and-chronic-poisoning?sectionName=Preventing+ongoing+exposure&topicRef=8365&anchor=H1562828577&source=see_link#H1562828577).)

Increased United States Emergency Department visits for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (December 2025)

Previous studies have reported rising rates of cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS), which causes episodic vomiting and intense abdominal pain in some individuals with prolonged, nearly daily cannabis use. A cross-sectional study of over 188 million United States emergency department (ED) visits found that from 2016 to 2020, visits for CHS sharply increased from 4 to 33 per 100,000 visits, and have since plateaued but remain elevated [[51](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/51)]. These findings highlight the medical burden of CHS, can help inform policy, and should remind ED clinicians to ask about cannabis use in patients with cyclic vomiting and abdominal pain. (See ["Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome", section on 'Epidemiology'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/cannabinoid-hyperemesis-syndrome?sectionName=EPIDEMIOLOGY&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2281824146&source=see_link#H2281824146).)

TRAUMA

PECARN cervical spine injury prediction rule performance by patient age (May 2026)

In a planned subanalysis of the cohort of 22,430 children used to develop the Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) Cervical Spine Injury (CSI) prediction rule ([algorithm 3](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)), age-specific rules were derived based on developmental transition (0 to <2 years, 2 to <8 years, 8 to <16 years, and 16 to <18 years) [[52](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/52)]. When compared with the PECARN CSI rule, testing characteristics were similar for the age-specific rules; the negative predictive value for the PECARN CSI rule (99.9 percent, prevalence of CSI 1.9 percent) equaled or exceeded all age-specific rules. These findings support the use of the PECARN CSI rule to determine the risk of CSI and the need for C-spine imaging in infants and children of all ages. (See ["Evaluation and acute management of cervical spine injuries in children and adolescents", section on 'Indications and choice of imaging'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-acute-management-of-cervical-spine-injuries-in-children-and-adolescents?sectionName=Indications+and+choice+of+imaging&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2844494741&source=see_link#H2844494741).)

Prehospital whole blood transfusion for traumatic hemorrhage (March 2026)

Two recent trials have examined the efficacy and safety of prehospital transfusion of low-titer, group O whole blood (LTOWB) versus blood components by Emergency Medical Services (EMS):

●In a pragmatic trial of over 600 patients with life-threatening bleeding transported by air ambulances in England, patients were transfused up to 2 units of LTOWB versus red cells plus plasma [[53](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/53)]. The composite of mortality plus massive transfusion within 24 hours and 90-day call-cause mortality was similar between the groups; the LTOWB group had slightly fewer serious adverse events.

●In another pragmatic trial of over 1000 patients with trauma and hypotension transported by air bases in the United States, either from the scene or from a referring emergency department, patients were transfused up to 2 units of LTOWB versus red cells, plasma, or both. Mortality at 30 days was similar (26 versus 21 percent) between LTOWB and components, as was in-hospital mortality, blood product requirements, and adverse events [[54](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/54)].

These findings suggest that use of LTOWB, which is logistically simpler than components, is a reasonable option for EMS with prehospital transfusion programs. (See ["Initial management of moderate to severe hemorrhage in the adult trauma patient", section on 'Transfusion'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/initial-management-of-moderate-to-severe-hemorrhage-in-the-adult-trauma-patient?sectionName=Transfusion&topicRef=8365&anchor=H749310297&source=see_link#H749310297).)

Comparison of C-spine injury prediction rules in children (January 2026)

The Pediatric Emergency Care Applied Research Network (PECARN) C-spine injury rule ([algorithm 3](https://www.uptodate.com/content-not-available)) demonstrates high accuracy for identifying C-spine injury in pediatric blunt trauma patients while lowering the use of computed tomography (CT) imaging, but evidence comparing it to other prediction rules commonly used in adult trauma centers is limited. A secondary analysis of the PECARN rule cohort (22,430 children) compared it with the National Emergency X-Radiography Utilization Study Low Risk (NEXUS) criteria and the Canadian Cervical Spine (C-spine) Rule (CCR) [[55](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/55)]. The results showed that the PECARN rule had higher sensitivity and negative predictive value for C-spine injury than the other two rules, with a lower projected CT imaging rate (PECARN 6.9 percent, NEXUS 10.8 percent, and CCR 13.2 percent). These findings support the use of the PECARN C-spine injury rule in children with blunt trauma rather than guidelines primarily or solely derived from adult patients. (See ["Evaluation and acute management of cervical spine injuries in children and adolescents", section on 'Indications and choice of imaging'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/evaluation-and-acute-management-of-cervical-spine-injuries-in-children-and-adolescents?sectionName=Indications+and+choice+of+imaging&topicRef=8365&anchor=H2844494741&source=see_link#H2844494741).)

Timing of tranexamic acid after trauma (December 2025)

Previous studies have found that [tranexamic acid](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/tranexamic-acid-drug-information?topicRef=8365&source=see_link) (TXA), an antifibrinolytic agent, reduces mortality if given within three hours of injury in patients with significant hemorrhage, but the greatest benefit may occur when TXA is given sooner. In a secondary analysis of the Prehospital Tranexamic Acid for Severe Trauma (PATCH-Trauma) trial, the 28-day mortality benefit was only present if TXA was administered within 90 minutes (17 percent TXA versus 25 percent placebo), while there was no benefit if administered between 90 and 180 minutes (18 percent TXA versus 17 percent placebo) [[56](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/whats-new-in-emergency-medicine/abstract/56)]. These findings suggest that the benefit of TXA is greatest if given early after injury. (See ["Initial management of moderate to severe hemorrhage in the adult trauma patient", section on 'Patient within three hours of injury'](https://www.uptodate.com/contents/initial-management-of-moderate-to-severe-hemorrhage-in-the-adult-trauma-patient?sectionName=Patient+within+three+hours+of+injury&topicRef=8365&anchor=H30549926&source=see_link#H30549926).)

# Managing Right Ventricular Failure in Pulmonary Embolism

Experience and evidence for the use of mechanical circulatory support for managing high-risk PE associated with shock.

By [Megan Burke, MD](https://citoday.com/search?q=megan+burke), and [Sameer J. Khandhar, MD](https://citoday.com/search?q=sameer+j+khandhar)

[View PDF](https://assets.bmctoday.net/citoday/pdfs/cit0323_SF2_Khandhar.pdf)[Reprints](https://citoday.com/reprints?f=https://citoday.com/articles/2023-mar-apr/managing-right-ventricular-failure-in-pulmonary-embolism)

[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Managing%20Right%20Ventricular%20Failure%20in%20Pulmonary%20Embolism%20on%20@cardiacinterv&url=https://citoday.com/articles/2023-mar-apr/managing-right-ventricular-failure-in-pulmonary-embolism)[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://citoday.com/articles/2023-mar-apr/managing-right-ventricular-failure-in-pulmonary-embolism&title=Managing%20Right%20Ventricular%20Failure%20in%20Pulmonary%20Embolism&description=Experience%20and%20evidence%20for%20the%20use%20of%20mechanical%20circulatory%20support%20for%20managing%20high-risk%20PE%20associated%20with%20shock.)[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://citoday.com/articles/2023-mar-apr/managing-right-ventricular-failure-in-pulmonary-embolism&title=Managing%20Right%20Ventricular%20Failure%20in%20Pulmonary%20Embolism&source=https://citoday.com/articles/2023-mar-apr/managing-right-ventricular-failure-in-pulmonary-embolism)[](mailto:?subject=Managing%20Right%20Ventricular%20Failure%20in%20Pulmonary%20Embolism&body=Check%20out%20this%20article%20from%20Cardiac%20Interventions%20Today:%20Managing%20Right%20Ventricular%20Failure%20in%20Pulmonary%20Embolism%20-%20https://citoday.com/articles/2023-mar-apr/managing-right-ventricular-failure-in-pulmonary-embolism "Share by Email")[](https://citoday.com/articles/2023-mar-apr/managing-right-ventricular-failure-in-pulmonary-embolism)

Every year in the United States, roughly 370,000 patients develop a pulmonary embolism (PE), with > 100,000 Americans dying annually from venous thromboembolic disease.1 The clinical significance of the PE depends on the right ventricular (RV) response to the clot and the increase in afterload. Patients with RV strain defined by positive biomarkers and RV enlargement are termed intermediate-high risk because they are at risk of progressing to shock. Those who present with cardiac arrest, hypotension, and evidence of end-organ hypoperfusion are termed high risk.2,3 Patients who progress to shock are associated with mortality rates of > 50%, making PE the third-leading cause of cardiovascular death after myocardial infarction (MI) and stroke.4 Although awareness and treatment options are improving, PE remains a significant public health problem.

During cardiogenic shock, mechanical circulatory support (MCS) serves as a bridge to maintain perfusion to the body long enough to allow for the correction of the underlying problem ([Figure 1](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig1.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 1.  MCS represented as a bridge to definitive treatment for PE.")). MCS use is ideal in scenarios in which there is an acute insult that is treatable, such as PE. Treatment options for PE have evolved beyond just anticoagulation and systemic thrombolytics to include surgical embolectomy and catheter-based percutaneous technologies.

[![Image 1](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig1.png?auto=compress,format)](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig1.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 1.  MCS represented as a bridge to definitive treatment for PE.")
Figure 1. MCS represented as a bridge to definitive treatment for PE.

In fact, our modern-day mechanical support devices are in a large part based on work done in the early 20th century after a patient died of PE. Dr. John Gibbon was a young surgeon in 1930 when he was tasked to care for a patient with a massive PE dying of progressive RV failure. Helplessly watching her pass away, he dedicated his research to developing a machine that would remove venous blood from the body, oxygenate this blood, and then return the blood to the arterial circulation, completely bypassing the cardiopulmonary system. By the late 1930s, he developed an extracorporeal oxygenation machine that gradually prolonged life from minutes to eventually weeks when the pulmonary artery was occluded. This technology allowed for more complex cardiac surgeries and served as the basis for future MCS devices.5

Although anticoagulation and systemic thrombolysis remain the standard for treatment per the guidelines, we are entering an era with rapid advancement of catheter-based technologies and MCS to treat PE. This article focuses on the use of MCS as part of the modern-day treatment armamentarium.

### MODERN-DAY THERAPY FOR PE

Anticoagulation remains the cornerstone therapy for treating all severities of PE. Anticoagulation prevents further clot formation while allowing the body’s own fibrinolysis to break down the clot, which can take time. Therefore, patients entering the shock spectrum often need a more rapid mechanism for clot reduction.

Systemic thrombolysis is the primary recommendation for high-risk PE patients based on American and European guidelines.2-6 This is based on historic data derived from older studies with small sample sizes. Meta-analyses have shown a benefit of systemic thrombolysis compared to anticoagulation alone,7-9 but significant limitations do exist and successful improvement in hemodynamics is not guaranteed. Limitations of thrombolysis include major bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, the inability to use in patients with contraindications, and higher rates of complications if MCS is needed afterward.

Due to the limitation of systemic thrombolysis, the concept of catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT)—in which a lower-dose thrombolytic agent is delivered directly into the pulmonary arteries—began to form. There are now several catheters designed for drug delivery into the pulmonary artery, leading to improvements in hemodynamics and RV function.10-14 To date, these studies primarily focused on intermediate-risk PE patients, with some successful data in sicker patients who are in shock. CDT can lead to significant hemodynamic improvements over the course of a few hours but prospective studies in high-risk PE are limited.13 The ease of insertion and rapid procedure time are major benefits but the true bleeding risk, the best delivery system, and optimal duration of infusion are still being investigated.

PE is caused by embolization of thrombus to the pulmonary artery and therefore it makes intuitive sense to develop tools to extract these clots as a form of treatment. Surgical thrombectomy achieves this but requires a sternotomy and is limited to surgeons with expertise. Several percutaneous devices now exist that allow for rapid extraction of large thrombus, with several more devices in development. [Figure 2](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig2.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 2.  Saddle PE on autopsy in a deceased patient (A). Saddle PE removed with large-bore MT using the Inari FlowTriever system (B).") demonstrates a saddle PE in a deceased patient and another patient in whom the saddle PE was successfully removed via mechanical thrombectomy (MT). These devices range from 8 to 24 F in size and can be performed via the jugular or femoral veins. These devices have been primarily studied in the intermediate-risk cohort,15-17 but the FlowTriever system (Inari Medical) was recently used in high-risk patients with success and low rates of complications.18,19 As the technology for thrombectomy improves so do the success rates of quickly removing large amounts of thrombus, leading to rapid hemodynamic improvements immediately during the procedure. High success rates, low complication rates, and an increase in the availability of these devices has made percutaneous thrombectomy more popular in the past several years. There are limited data comparing these devices and use depends on institutional expertise.

[![Image 2](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig2.png?auto=compress,format)](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig2.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 2.  Saddle PE on autopsy in a deceased patient (A). Saddle PE removed with large-bore MT using the Inari FlowTriever system (B).")
Figure 2. Saddle PE on autopsy in a deceased patient (A). Saddle PE removed with large-bore MT using the Inari FlowTriever system (B).

### CRITERIA FOR MCS

We have defined criteria for cardiogenic shock and for high-risk PE but now recognize that shock is a continuum. Patients can present at various points on the shock spectrum, making it clinically quite difficult to determine when a massive PE patient will require MCS. Systemic thrombolysis remains the mainstay therapy for high-risk PE patients despite known limitations and incomplete success rates. We do administer systemic thrombolysis in patients in early shock or on low-dose vasopressors before they progress to worsening shock or cardiac arrest. The use of MCS after systemic thrombolysis is associated with significant bleeding risk. Therefore, for those with more advanced shock, we prefer to avoid systemic thrombolysis and instead move forward with the combination of MCS and a definitive catheter-based treatment strategy.

MCS is associated with considerable cost and risk, so it is prudent to use these devices in appropriate patients. This is one of the reasons why hospitals have adopted PE response teams to provide a multidisciplinary localized approach to care for these complex patients.20 We advocate for MCS before cardiac arrest, and once a patient has been temporarily stabilized on MCS, to proceed with a more definitive PE treatment.

### TYPES OF MCS

RV support can be looked at in terms of maximizing RV preload, afterload, and contractility as shown in [Figure 3](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig3.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 3.  RV support in terms of maximizing preload, afterload, and contractility."). Although afterload and contractility can be improved somewhat with medical therapy, RV support devices provide more complete cardiac output in sicker patients. The three current devices to assist with RV failure include the Impella RP device (Abiomed, Inc.), the ProtekDuo system (LivaNova), and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). Each device has certain benefits and limitations when used specifically for PE. There are several other pumps that can be configured with a cannula in the right atrium and a cannula in the pulmonary artery to achieve RV support, but most cardiologists use the commercially available ones.

[![Image 3](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig3.png?auto=compress,format)](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig3.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 3.  RV support in terms of maximizing preload, afterload, and contractility.")
Figure 3. RV support in terms of maximizing preload, afterload, and contractility.

The Impella RP device is a 23-F axial flow pump placed through a percutaneous approach from the femoral vein. This device pushes blood from the inferior vena cava (IVC)/right atrium into the pulmonary arteries. This motor is contained in the body with only the driveline exiting the femoral vein. This device provides up to 4 L/minute of blood flow. Limitations of the device are that it cannot be placed from the jugular vein and an oxygenator cannot be added if hypoxia occurs. Published data for the use of the Impella RP in PE are limited to small case series but have shown hemodynamic improvements when combined with a more definitive PE therapy.21,22 This device seems best suited for patients who have undergone a successful clot reduction treatment but have persistent RV failure without hypoxemia. The benefits of this device in a patient with a large burden of ongoing thrombus is not clear, and it seems likely best to avoid pumping a high flow into obstructed pulmonary arteries. [Figure 4](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig4.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 4.  Example of Impella RP device placed via the femoral artery and into the pulmonary artery.") shows the placement of the Impella RP in a patient with persistent RV failure after completing a course of CDT.

[![Image 4](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig4.png?auto=compress,format)](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig4.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 4.  Example of Impella RP device placed via the femoral artery and into the pulmonary artery.")
Figure 4. Example of Impella RP device placed via the femoral artery and into the pulmonary artery.

The ProtekDuo is a 29- or 31-F dual-lumen catheter placed via the internal jugular vein into the pulmonary artery. The inflow cannula in the right atrium removes blood from the body, where an external pump then ejects the blood through the outflow lumen to the pulmonary artery. Because the pump is external to the body, an oxygenator can be easily added before blood is returned to the pulmonary artery. Similar to the Impella RP device, use seems to be best in patients with residual RV failure after there has been clot reduction in the pulmonary arteries. Small case series have been published but large-scale studies in PE have not been performed.23[Figure 5](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig5.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 5.  Example of a ProtekDuo device placed via the right internal jugular vein into the pulmonary artery.") illustrates the ProtekDuo system.

[![Image 5](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig5.png?auto=compress,format)](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig5.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 5.  Example of a ProtekDuo device placed via the right internal jugular vein into the pulmonary artery.")
Figure 5. Example of a ProtekDuo device placed via the right internal jugular vein into the pulmonary artery.

Peripheral ECMO remains the most popular MCS system in high-risk PE patients.24,25 Venoarterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) removes blood from the jugular and/or IVC veins, where it is oxygenated in an external circuit before being pumped back into the body via the femoral artery into the aorta. VA-ECMO is designed to completely bypass the heart and lungs, and therefore a definitive clot reduction therapy is not immediately necessary.

The use of VA-ECMO has significantly grown worldwide as availability has increased, but rapid initiation remains a limitation at many centers. This device does provide full cardiopulmonary support but requires large-bore arterial access, which is associated with higher complication rates of bleeding and distal limb ischemia. Initiation and cannulation for VA-ECMO shortly after a patient has undergone systemic thrombolysis is associated with very high rates of bleeding given the large-bore arterial access required. In patients with profound shock or cardiac arrest, we favor VA-ECMO for support before administering systemic thrombolysis. Once patients are supported with VA-ECMO, a more definitive therapy for their PE can be undertaken.

Although most patients with high-risk PE will have hemodynamic impact, there is a group of PE patients in whom severe hypoxemia is the primary problem. In these patients, the use of venovenous ECMO (VV-ECMO) can be considered. VV-ECMO is when blood is removed from the right side of the heart, sent to an oxygenator, and then returned back into the right side. Access is achieved in two large veins without simultaneous arterial access. The oxygenated blood requires intrinsic RV function to move blood through the pulmonary circulation and to the left heart.

There are no true head-to-head studies with these devices in acute PE. The choice of device therefore depends on institutional availability and comfort. The Impella PR and ProtekDuo systems can be placed quickly without the need for a perfusionist. ECMO can be more labor-intensive, requiring a perfusionist, but does offer more complete cardiopulmonary support.

### COMBINING MCS AND CATHETER-BASED THERAPIES

Historically, systemic thrombolysis was the treatment recommendation for high-risk PE patients, but we know that thrombolytics are frequently withheld due to contraindications or fear of causing a bleeding event.26 In addition, combining MCS and systemic thrombolysis can also be associated with high bleeding and complication rates.

How best to combine MCS with these newer catheter-based therapies and how they complement each other is still being investigated. Initial studies for CDT and MT started in the intermediate-risk category. As the technology improved and operator comfort increased, these devices began to be applied in sicker high-risk PE patients.11,18,19 We believe we are entering an era in which the optimal treatment for high-risk PE is evolving, similar to what occurred in MI and stroke to include MCS and catheter-based interventions. MCS could serve as a mechanism of support to bridge patients to a catheter-based therapy and recovery ([Figure 1](https://core4-cms.imgix.net/issue-2402/0323_SF2_Fig1.png?auto=compress,format "Figure 1.  MCS represented as a bridge to definitive treatment for PE.")). The FLAME study is the latest and largest prospective trial conducted in the modern era for high-risk PE and will serve as the basis for ongoing studies.18

### TIPS AND TRICKS FOR USING MCS IN HIGH-RISK PE

Use of the Impella RP and ProtekDuo is limited to small case series, and use at our institution has also been limited to a small cohort of select patients. Both devices can be placed in the cardiac catheterization laboratory or operating room without the need for a perfusionist. Our choice between these two devices is based on access location (jugular vs femoral vein) and the need for additional oxygenation. We have also used this device primarily in patients who have ongoing RV shock after treatment with MT or CDT so that the pulmonary arteries are patent to allow for the transit of blood to the left heart.

Our institutional preference to treat PE shock is VA-ECMO because this provides full cardiopulmonary support. We fortunately have a perfusionist available full time to support these patients, making it a readily available option. Placement of VA-ECMO can occur in the emergency department, catheterization laboratory, operating room, or at the bedside in the intensive care unit by interventional cardiology, cardiac surgery, or anesthesia critical care.

We have placed VA-ECMO several times in patients we suspect are in shock due to a PE but are too unstable for a CT scan. Once the patient has been stabilized on VA-ECMO we will then proceed with a CT scan with PE protocol. It is important to remember to turn down the ECMO flow rate at the time of the CT scan to get an accurate scan. If ECMO flow rates are high, the opacification of the pulmonary artery with the intravenous contrast bolus will be incomplete and the diagnosis of PE can be missed.

There are data from France suggesting that high-risk PE patients can be supported for several days while being anticoagulated with heparin to allow for the body’s intrinsic hemolytic system to break down the clot.27 Our preference is once a patient is stable on VA-ECMO to proceed with a catheter-based intervention to shorten the ECMO duration and promote RV recovery. The choice of CDT or MT in these patients has to do with patient characteristics, if they have any contraindications to catheter-delivered thrombolytics, and the location of the clot. We prefer CDT in those patients with more distal segment and subsegment level clot that can be harder to reach with MT. This oftentimes happens if the patient underwent CPR in which the chest compressions can fragment the clot, leading it to move more distal. CDT involves 5- to 7-F venous access and can be done on full ECMO support without significant risk of air embolization. With the slow infusion of alteplase at 1 mg per hour, we have not noted higher bleeding rates compared to ECMO alone at our institution.

We prefer MT for larger more central clots that are obstructing the main pulmonary arteries. We have successfully performed MT in patients on VA-ECMO, but there are several steps unique to when both are done together. Because this is a large-bore venous access, it is important to turn the VA-ECMO flows down when the large sheath is inserted into the venous system and each time the device is introduced through the large-bore sheath to avoid air entrainment. When performing MT in conjunction with VA-ECMO, we have the perfusionist in the cardiac catheterization lab and will ask them to turn the flow rate down as low as tolerated each time the catheter is inserted. Once the catheter is in place, we will return to full ECMO flow while the thrombectomy is being performed. When we remove the catheter or return the extra aspirated blood back to the patient, we once again lower the ECMO flow rates. This communication is critical to avoid air entrainment and embolization complications.

Another concern early on was the ability for the IVC to accommodate the ECMO venous cannula and the large-bore sheath for MT if using the FlowTriever system. The IVC is compliant and oftentimes quite dilated in these patients with RV failure, making placement of both devices possible via the femoral veins. In smaller patients, we would consider accessing the jugular and femoral veins to allow for VA-ECMO from one site and MT from the other.

### CONCLUSION

PE is the third-leading cause of cardiovascular death after acute MI and stroke, so improving outcomes in these patients is a public health priority. The treatment for high-risk PE is evolving beyond anticoagulation and systemic thrombolysis, with mechanical support and catheter-based therapies providing alternative strategies. The current data for MCS and catheter-based therapies are not yet sufficient to make a definitive guideline-level recommendation. Nonetheless, we may be at the early stages of a paradigm shift for high-risk PE, similar to what previously occurred in treatment for MI.

FEBRUARY 2024  | VOLUME 26  | ISSUE 2 

# Emergency Department 

# Management of Patients 

# With Right Heart Failure 

n Abstract 

Right heart failure (RHF) can result from many cardiac, pulmonary, 

and systemic pathologies. Common causes of RHF include 

pulmonary embolism, left heart failure, congenital heart disease, 

chronic lung disease, acute myocardial infarction, infiltrative 

disease, infectious disease, and valvular abnormalities. Acute 

and chronic RHF confer a high risk for morbidity and mortality 

in the acute care setting, and interventions commonly used in 

emergency care can prompt acute decompensation if the RHF 

is not recognized. The severity of presentation may range from 

compensated clinically silent cardiovascular dysfunction to venous 

congestion, multiorgan failure, and circulatory collapse. This review 

describes the pathophysiology of right heart failure and offers an 

evidence-based approach to the diagnosis, management, and 

disposition of both acute and chronic RHF. 

EBMEDICINE.NET This issue is eligible for CME credit. See page 2. 

CLINICAL CHALLENGES: 

• What are the primary etiologies of 

right heart failure (RHF)? 

• Which diagnostic studies should 

be ordered for patients with 

suspected RHF? 

• What are the most effective 

treatment strategies for RHF, 

based on underlying etiologies?

# Case Presentations 

n Introduction 

Right heart failure (RHF) is the common endpoint of 

numerous cardiac, pulmonary, and systemic patholo -

gies, and can present a high risk for patient morbidity 

and mortality in the acute care setting. Presentation 

severity runs a spectrum from compensated, clinically 

silent cardiovascular dysfunction to venous conges -

tion, multiorgan failure, and circulatory collapse. 1

While RHF is common among emergency de -

partment (ED) patients, diagnosing and managing 

RHF is challenging. 1 Specific hurdles include etio -

logic heterogeneity, nonspecific clinical presenta -

tions, comorbid complexity, potentially harmful 

effects of common ED treatments, and a limited 

armamentarium of diagnostic and therapeutic tools 

available to ED clinicians. The presence of RHF can 

dramatically alter the risk-benefit profile of manage -

ment and disposition paradigms for common ED 

conditions, making recognition of RHF vitally impor -

tant. This issue of  Emergency Medicine Practice  pres -

ents an evidence-based approach to the diagnosis, 

management, and disposition of patients with RHF. 

n Selected Abbreviations

COPD  Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

n Etiology and Pathophysiology 

Right heart function is dictated by 3 basic physiologic 

domains: (1) resistance to right ventricular ejection 

(afterload) via pulmonary artery pressure; (2) right 

ventricular systolic and diastolic pump function; and 

(3) right heart filling (preload) via systemic venous 

return.  (See Figure 1.)  The pathophysiology of RHF 

can be conceptualized by the affected domain: 

increased afterload (pulmonary hypertension), 

reduced right ventricular contractility or compliance, 

and/or excess preload (volume excess, elevated 

central venous pressure). 1 At the “tipping point” 

from compensated to decompensated RHF, typically 

all 3 domains are impaired, due to self-propagating 

feedback loops wherein dysfunction of any single 

domain precipitates worsening of the other domains. 

(See Figure 2, page 5.) 

Pulmonary hypertension is associated with nearly 

all etiologies of RHF. 1 The thin-walled right ventricle 

is profoundly afterload-sensitive compared to the 

left ventricle, since mean pulmonary artery pres -

sure is normally minimal (<25 mm Hg) compared 

to aortic pressures. Therefore, only small increases 

in afterload are necessary to cause acute or chronic 

RHF. Pulmonary hypertension can develop as a 

progressive chronic disease and/or by rapid severe 

decompensation and is categorized by 5 etiological 

“groups.”  (See Table 1, page 6.)  Acute pulmonary 

vascular obstruction (eg, pulmonary embolism) and 

hypoxemic vasoconstriction of pulmonary vessels 

are 2 of the fastest and most dramatic mechanisms 

behind rapid elevation of pulmonary artery pressure

Right Ventricular Myocardial Infarction 

RHF due to acute right ventricular myocardial infarc -

tion (RVMI) should be suspected in patients with 

hypotension, jugular venous distension, clear lung 

fields, and symptoms consistent with acute myocar -

dial ischemia. Isolated RVMI is uncommon (3% of 

all myocardial infarctions [MIs]), but right ventricular 

ischemia complicated up to half of all inferior MIs 

in a retrospective study of 232 patients. 10  Heart 

failure is common after RVMI and can worsen its 

clinical course. 2 Moreover, as many as one-third of 

anterior acute MIs may result in RVD. 11  RVMI dispro -

portionately accounts for acute MIs complicated by 

cardiogenic shock and a high burden of arrythmias. 1

Causes of Acute Right Heart Failure 

Acute Pulmonary Embolism 

Pulmonary embolism is the most common cause of 

acute RHF. Lower extremity deep vein thrombi, and 

less commonly other products (amniotic fluid, air, or 

septic emboli), embolize to the pulmonary arterial tree 

and obstruct circulatory flow. Obstruction rapidly in -

creases right ventricular afterload, often proportionally 

to total clot burden and clot location. 6,7 The increased 

afterload is sufficient to cause RVD and acute RHF in 

50% to 60% of pulmonary emboli, and overt obstruc -

tive shock in 5% to 10%. 8 RHF is the primary source of 

morbidity and mortality in pulmonary embolism. 6,7

Sepsis 

In a prospective study of 252 septic ED patients, 

34% of patients with sepsis or septic shock exhib -

ited RVD, occurring with concomitant left ventricu -

lar systolic dysfunction in 71% of those patients. 9

Pathophysiology is poorly understood and may 

represent a combination of “unmasked” underly -

ing cardiac disease, de novo septic cardiomyopathy 

due to inflammatory and neurohormonal cascades, 

secondary effects of multiorgan dysfunction (eg, 

renal and hepatic failure, acute respiratory distress 

syndrome [ARDS]), and iatrogenic effects of common 

interventions (aggressive intravenous [IV] volume 

loading, positive pressure ventilation (PPV) and acute 

cor pulmonale). 1 Signs and symptoms of RHF overlap 

with multiorgan dysfunction in sepsis, and patients 

with RVD have dramatically poorer outcomes than 

those without. 9

Severe COVID-19 infection is associated with acute

Causes of Chronic Right Heart Failure 

Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension 

Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension 

(CTEPH) is a chronic disease wherein persistent pul -

monary vascular obstruction leads to chronic pulmo -

nary hypertension and RHF. It is thought that chronic 

residual thrombus may undergo fibrous organization, 

which renders it less susceptible to treatment by 

thrombolysis. 18  An estimated 4% to 12% of patients 

in a retrospective cohort of 358 patients with acute 

pulmonary embolism developed CTEPH. 18  A substan -

tial proportion of CTEPH cases occur in the absence 

an inserted cardiac device. In a retrospective cohort 

of 939 patients, occlusions proximal to the right 

ventricle marginal artery were associated with larger 

infarction size and higher rates of cardiogenic shock 

and mortality. 12 

Positive Pressure Ventilation and Acute 

Respiratory Distress Syndrome 

Invasive PPV increases intrathoracic pressure, 

which may compress the pulmonary vasculature 

and increase right ventricular afterload. Elevated 

intrathoracic pressure also reduces central venous 

return, causing decreased right ventricular preload. 

In patients with impaired right ventricular function, 

depressed right ventricular preload can improve 

hemodynamics for those who are volume/pressure 

overloaded, or it can precipitate hemodynamic col -

lapse in patients who are euvolemic or hypovolemic. 

(See Figure 3.) 

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome 

In a retrospective study of 583 patients, acute 

RHF was a complication of ARDS in 25% to 50% 

of cases. 13  The effects of PPV are compounded by 

hypoxia and permissive hypercapnia contributing to 

pulmonary vasoconstriction. The high positive end-

expiratory pressure (PEEP) strategy commonly used 

in ARDS leads to increased right ventricular afterload 

and decreased right ventricular preload, worsening 

right heart function. A single-center retrospective 

review of 352 patients with ARDS showed mortality

failure, 53% of patients had RVD and/or pulmonary

n=50) progression to CTEPH was more common

echocardiography (TTE) after treatment for acute pul -

The criteria for CTEPH are based on elevated per -

sistent right ventricular pressures, and right-heart cath -

eterization is typically necessary for diagnosis. Com -

puted tomographic pulmonary angiography (CTPA) 

is insufficient to exclude the diagnosis. 4 Diagnostic 

criteria also include persistent pulmonary hypertension 

for at least 3 months on appropriate anticoagulation 

therapy to differentiate CTEPH from “subacute” pul -

hypertension. 4 Patients with unexplained pulmonary 

hypertension and/or chronic RHF with or without a his -

gent referral to a pulmonary hypertension specialist for 

diagnosis. 4 CTEPH is one of the few causes of chronic 

pulmonary hypertension for which etiology-specific 

therapy (pulmonary endarterectomy) can be effective 

at reversing the disease. 4

n Prehospital Care 

Given the difficulty in diagnosing RHF without TTE, 

specific, directed care for RHF in the prehospital set -

ting may be challenging. For patients at risk for RHF 

based on history, prehospital providers should avoid 

interventions that could worsen RVD and precipitate 

cardiac arrest, including intubation, phenylephrine, 

and large IV fluid boluses. 4

n Emergency Department Evaluation 

History 

The first step in ED evaluation for RHF is a thorough 

history and chart review, with emphasis on risk factors 

that could predispose the patient to chronic or acute-

on-chronic RHF.  (See Table 1, page 6.)  Next, clini -

cians should identify whether any of a patient’s acute 

conditions diagnosed during standard ED workup are 

associated with acute or acute-on-chronic RHF.  (See 

Table 4.)  Acute RHF most commonly occurs in the 

caring for patients with congenital heart disease is un -

derstanding the patient-specific anatomy and physi -

ological adaptations. 

RHF is a common late complication of congenital 

heart disease, occurring decades after initial repair 

in 5% to 10% of patients. 4 Among congenital heart 

disease patients hospitalized for heart failure as 

adults, two-thirds show signs of RHF. 23  Mortality in 

this population may, nevertheless, be similar to other 

patients hospitalized for acute heart failure. 23  Acute 

evaluation with TTE can be helpful (even though the 

distorted anatomy may be challenging to interpret) 

because it can yield information regarding volume 

status and ventricular function. Detailed descriptions 

of specific forms of congenital heart disease and their 

ED management are beyond the scope of this review, 

but may be found in other resources. 24 

Left Ventricular Assist Devices 

Right ventricular failure is one of the most common 

complications post-LVAD implantation. LVAD implan -

tation improves contractility and forward flow from 

the left ventricle, which decreases right ventricular 

afterload. However, increasing cardiac output also 

increases systemic venous return, which may over -

load a weakened right ventricle. In a single-center 

retrospective study of 293 patients, 11% of patients 

were found to have late RHF after LVAD implantation, 

which was associated with a 15% absolute reduction 

in survival. 25 

Lung Diseases and Group 3 Pulmonary 

Hypertension 

RHF due to acute or chronic lung disease, known as 

cor pulmonale , occurs secondary to pulmonary vas -

cular constriction, chronic hypoxia/hypercapnia, and/ 

or loss of pulmonary vascular beds. Ultimately, these 

factors lead to increased right ventricular afterload 

and subsequent isolated right ventricular failure. A 

wide array of obstructive and restrictive lung diseases 

can lead to this pathophysiology.  (See Table 1, page 

6.)  Many etiologies present with acute-on-chronic 

decompensation, while others can complicate unre -

lated ED presentations as chronic risk factors. 

Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension 

Pulmonary arterial hypertension is an idiopathic 

increase in pulmonary artery tone and resistance. The 

most common complication of these changes is RHF. 1

Pulmonary arterial hypertension is the only chronic 

cause of pulmonary hypertension for which chronic 

pulmonary vasodilator therapy is universally beneficial 

as a disease-modifying therapy, and discontinuation 

of these home medications can rapidly precipitate 

acute-on-chronic RHF.

Historical symptoms consistent with RHF are 

largely the same as for isolated left-sided heart 

failure: dyspnea, chest pain, fatigue, exercise intoler -

ance, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and 

edema. Edema is often the most prominent factor in 

chronic RHF, but may be minimal or absent in acute 

RHF. 1 Anorexia, abdominal bloating, cachexia, and 

early satiety occur in RHF due to splanchnic conges -

tion, but are also more common with chronicity. 

Syncope in a patient with confirmed acute pulmo -

nary embolism is relatively specific for RHF, though it 

lacked sensitivity in a prospective trial of 335 pa -

tients. 26  Unfortunately, no symptoms are highly sensi -

tive or specific for RHF. 1,27 

A new diagnosis of RHF/pulmonary hyperten -

sion should also be considered when a patient has 

dyspnea or fatigue that cannot be attributed to 

comorbidities. In a prospective cohort of 83 ED 

patients, 20% to 30% of those with negative CTPA 

performed for shortness of breath had undiagnosed 

isolated RHF. 28 

Physical Examination 

No physical examination signs are sensitive or specific 

for RHF. The findings that clinicians associate with 

left-sided heart failure are essentially the same as 

those in RHF, including jugular venous distention, 

hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, and abdominal 

distention. 1 Society guidelines suggest that a lack of 

pulmonary edema with other signs of heart failure 

can suggest isolated right ventricle failure, though 

this pattern has not been examined in the literature 

and is thought to lack both sensitivity and specificity, 

since nearly half of heart failure is biventricular. 

Unfortunately, auscultation lacks significant accuracy 

for diagnosing pulmonary edema. 1,22 

n Diagnostic Studies 

Biomarkers 

Laboratory studies are useful in screening for RHF, 

but they lack specificity for confirming the diagnosis. 

Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP), N-terminal pro-brain 

natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP), and troponin are 

secreted by the myocardium in response to increased 

ventricular pressure and volume. Thus, as with history 

and physical examination findings, biomarker eleva -

tions will be present in both right and left heart failure. 

Biomarkers of renal function can help diagnose 

cardiorenal syndrome, which is characterized 

clinically by decreased urine output, fluid retention, 

and increased diuretic requirements. Cardiorenal 

syndrome is typically a result of increased central 

venous pressure, in which elevated renal vein 

pressure impairs renal perfusion, and therefore 

is commonly a result of RHF. 1 (See Figure 4.)

ECG is nonspecific and insensitive for RHF diagnosis. 

However, combination of many signs may additively 

enhance diagnostic performance. In a prospective 

study of 103 patients with pulmonary embolism, an 

“ECG score” of 17 different signs achieved 0.82 area 

under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 

TTE evidence of RVD, although this scoring system 

has not been externally validated. 29 

Transthoracic Echocardiography 

Although TTE is the primary diagnostic modality for 

confirming the presence or absence of RHF, signs of 

RHF on TTE are nonspecific for underlying etiologies 

of RHF. 5,31  TTE is rapid, noninvasive, and can be per -

formed at the bedside. Although no single TTE pa -

rameter defines RHF and multiple parameters may be 

interpreted in concert, commonly used measures— 

including the ratio of the sizes of the right ventricle to 

the left ventricle (RV/LV), and tricuspid annular plane 

systolic excursion (TAPSE)—can provide reasonable 

global assessments of RVD. Novice emergency clini -

cian sonographers show strong correlation in acqui -

sition and interpretation of these 2 measures when 

compared to formal echocardiography interpreted 

by cardiologists, with kappa 0.68 (95% CI, 0.48-0.88) 

for right ventricular dilation and 0.94 (95% CI, 0.87-

0.98) for TAPSE. 22 ,30-34  A normal RV/LV ratio should 

be <0.8, with larger ratios suggesting right ventricular 

pressure overload. The RV/LV ratio is most accurately 

measured in the apical 4-chamber view just above the 

tips of the tricuspid and mitral valves.  (See Figure 6, 

page 12.)  Generally, a ratio >1 is pathologic. In 2 ret -

rospective studies (n=161 and n=1416), progressively 

higher values had higher specificity for pathology. 35 ,36 

A major pitfall of the RV/LV ratio is its lack of effec -

tiveness in biventricular disease, since both ventricles FEBRUARY 2024  • www.ebmedicine.net  12 ©2024 EB MEDICINE 

may be enlarged proportionally. In biventricular dis -

ease, measuring right ventricular end-diastolic diam -

eter may be more effective, with measurements >4.2 

cm representing elevated right ventricular pressure. 

TAPSE measures the vertical movement of the lat -

eral annulus of the tricuspid valve across the cardiac 

cycle. As much as 80% of right ventricular contraction 

occurs in the apical-basal plane. In a meta-analysis 

of 81 studies, greater vertical movement of the valve 

annulus was correlated with greater right ventricu -

lar systolic function. 37  To measure TAPSE, an apical 

4-chamber view is obtained with M-mode crossing 

the lateral tricuspid annulus, and measurement is per -

formed at the peak and trough of the waveform.  (See 

Figure 7.)  TAPSE values <17 mm are concerning for 

significant RVD and, in multiple prospective observa -

tional trials, were associated with worse outcomes in 

conditions including pulmonary embolism and acute 

heart failure. 22 ,31 ,38 ,39 

While TAPSE is a generally robust measure of 

overall right ventricular systolic function, it can be 

falsely normal in patients with severe chronic pulmo -

nary hypertension. As the right ventricle remodels in 

chronic pulmonary hypertension, a greater propor -

tion of right ventricular stroke volume comes from 

contraction in the lateral-septal plane as opposed to 

the typical apical-basal plane. Thus, when the right 

ventricle is chronically dilated due to long-standing 

severe pulmonary hypertension, TAPSE may be falsely 

preserved (ie, normal) in the presence of RHF.

Right ventricular end-diastolic diameter >4.2 cm 

suggests elevated right ventricular pressures. 41  (See 

Figure 8.)  Right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) 

which, in most circumstances, equals pulmonary 

artery systolic pressure (PASP), is estimated from the 

maximum velocity of the tricuspid regurgitant jet 

(present in approximately 90% of the healthy popula -

tion) 1 on continuous-wave Doppler. Peak tricuspid 

regurgitant jet velocity >2.8 meters/sec is abnormal, 

and RVSP (PASP) is equal to 4 times this velocity 

squared. 41  (See Figure 8.)  Many ultrasound machines 

facilitate automatic calculation of RVSP. Pulsed-wave 

Doppler of the pulmonic valve/right ventricular out -

flow tract can also suggest elevated pulmonary artery 

pressures. A mid-systolic notch in this waveform or 

a time to peak acceleration of <90 milliseconds is 

highly specific for elevated mean pulmonary artery 

pressure. Tracing the right ventricle chamber areas at 

end-systole and end-diastole in an apical view and 

calculating the percent difference yields right ven -

tricular fractional area change, which is an alternative 

measure of right ventricular systolic function, with an 

abnormal cutoff at <35%. 41 

Right atrial pressure is estimated by inferior vena 

cava maximum diameter and collapsibility, just proxi -

mal to the junction of the hepatic vein and inferior 

vena cava. 41  (See Figure 9, page 14.)  Two cutoffs are 

relevant: maximum inferior vena cava diameter ≥2.1 

cm, and inferior vena cava respiratory collapsibility of 

≤50%. If both are true, right atrial pressure is elevated 

(≥15 mm Hg, range 10-20 mm Hg); if both are false, 

right atrial pressure is normal (3 mm Hg, range 0-5 mm 

Hg). 41  Otherwise, right atrial pressure is indetermi -

nate (8 mm Hg; range, 5-10 mm Hg). Compared with 

invasive measures, this estimation is highly accurate at 

values that are low (3 mm Hg) and high (15 mm Hg), 

but less so when indeterminate (8 mm Hg), or in the 

presence of invasive positive pressure ventilation. 41

CT is essential in diagnosis of acute pulmonary em -

without acute pulmonary embolism. 44  This suggests 

that not only is an elevated RV/LV ratio common 

on CT, but also may reflect a patient’s underlying 

comorbidities rather than the pulmonary embolism. 44

varying utility and/or feasibility. Retrospective data
